IS LIFE WORTFI LIVING? ' Life not worth living! Come with me, Now that, through vanishing veil. Shimmers the dew on lawn and lea, And milk foams in the pail; :Now that June's sweltering sunlight bathes With sweat the striplings lithe, As fall the long straight scented swathes Over the rhythmic scythe; Now that the throstle never stops His self-sufficing strain, And woodbine-trails festoon the copse, And eglantine the lane; Now rustic hbour seems as sweet As leisure, and blithe herds Wend homeward with unweary feet, Carolling like the birds ; Now all, except the lover's vow, And nightingale, is still; Here, in the starlit hour, allow, Lite is worth living still. When Summer, lingering half-forlorn, On Autumn loves to lean, And fields of slowly yellowing corn Are girt by woods still green; When hazel-nuts wax brown and plump, And apples rosy-red, And the owlet hoots from hollow stump, And the dormouse makes its bed; When crAmmed are all the granary di:aka, And the Hunter's moon is bright, And life again is sweet indoors, And logs again alight; Ay. even when the houseless wind Waileth through cleft and chink, ' And in the twilight maids grow kind, And jugs are filled and clink; When children clasp their hands and pray, "Be done Thy heavenly will!" Who doth not lift his voice, and say, "Life is worth living still"? Not care to live while English homes ',- Nestle in English trees, And England's Trident-ceptre roams Her territorial seas! Not, live while English songs are sung Wherever blows the wind, And England's laws and England's tongue Enfranchise half mankind ! So long as in PaCifif! main, Or on Atlantic strand, Our kin transmit the parent strain. And love the Mother Land; So long as in this ocean Realm, Victoria and her Line Retain the heritage of the helm, By loyalty divine; So long as fiashas English steel, And Enr,lish trumpets shrill, Be is dead already who doth not feel Lite is worth living stilL —English Illustrated.

-- Vanity keeps persons in favour with themselves,:who are out of favonr with all others. What is the difference between a gaoler and a jeweller? —The one watches cells, and the other sells watches. "This coffee is very muddy this morning." "Yes, dear, but you must remember how upset things are in
Brazil." - "Dignity, my son, is a very proper sort of :a thing; but don't put on too much of it, or you tr ay be taken

for a footnian." One of the Seven was wont to say that laws were like cobwebs, where the small flies were caught and the great broke through. First boy (in surprise): "Why. I heard you ran off to join a circus. Didn't yon catch it?" Second boy: "Not till I got back home." No man ever lived a right life who had not been chastened by a woman's love, strengthened by her courage. and guided by her discretion. Mr. Popham, when he was Speaker, and the Lower House had sat long, and done in effect nothing, coming one day to Queen Elizabeth, she said to him, "Now, Mr. Speaker, what has passed in the Lower House?" He answered, "If it please your Majesty, seven weeks." In a small country town a minister closed his sermon the other day with these words: "We would be pleased, moreover, to have the young man who is now standing outside the door come in and make certain whether she is here or not. That would be a great deal better than opening the door half an inch and expesing the people in the last row of Feats to a draught." The Rev. Dr. Sutton once said to the late Mr. Peech, a veterinary surgeon, "Mr. Peech, how is it that you have not called upon me for your account?" "Oh," said Mr. Peech, "I never ask a gentleman for money !" "In- deed !" said the vicar. '" Then how do you get on if he doesn't pay?" "Why," replied Mr. Peech, "after a certain time I conclude that he is not a gentleman, and then I ask him." " said the grey-eved wayfarer at the railway refreshment-room," this is the old place. I recognised yonder landmark at once." "What landmark ?" in- quired the barmaid, considerately. "Two years ago, when I travelled over this line," continued the stranger, in a choking voice, "I carved my initials and the date on yonder bun. I see you have it still. Eicuse an old man's tears." Stranger (driving past the foot of a mountain; to driver): "Anything remarkable about this mountain?" Driver: "There is nothing peculiar about the; hill itself, but there's a queer story connected with it." Stranger: "What is that ?" Driver: "A young lady? and gentle- man went out for a walk on this hill; they ascended higher and higher and—never came back . again." Stranger: "Dear me! What, then, had become: of the unhappy pair?" Driver: "They went down on the other side." A kilted Highlander wss in the habit of walking to the nearest town—six miles off—for his provisions. Baying on one occasion purchased some matches, he found on return home that they were useless. On his next visit to the town he took them back, and complained to the grocer's assistant that they would not light. The latter, taking one, drew it in American fashion across his nether garments, and the match caught fire. But this demonstration, instead of satisfying the Highlander, angered him the more. "And wha." he cried. "is going to travel twelve miles to light the matches on your breeks?" FRIDAY.—Lee surrendered on Friday. Moscow was burned on Friday. Washington was born on Friday. Shakspere was born on Friday. America was discovered on Friday. Richmond was evacuated on Friday. The Bastile was destroyed on Friday. The Mayflower was landed on Friday. Queen Victoria was married on Friday. King Charles I. was beheaded on Friday. Fort Sumter was bombarded on Friday. Napoleon Bonaparte was born on Friday. Julius Cresar was assassinated on Friday. The battle of Marengo was fought on Friday. The battle of Bunker Hill was fought on Friday. Joan of Arc was burned at the stake orr Friday. The battle of New Orleans was fought on Friday. The Declaration of American Independence was signed on Friday. PAPA AND Tits BM—Charming as is the merry prattle off innocent childhood, it is not particularly agreeable about one o'clock in the morning, when you are "dead for sleep," and wouldn't give a copper to hear even Gladstone himself talk. There are young and talkative children, who have no more regard for your feelings, or the proprieties of life than to open their peepers with a snap at one or two a.m., and to seek to engage 'you in enlivening dialogues of this sort : " Papa !I' You think you will pay no heed to the im- perative little voice, hoping that silence on your part will keep the youngster quiet, but again the boy of three pipes out sharply," Pape. !" "Well?" you say. "You 'wake, papa?" "Yes." 6' So's me." "Yes, I hear that you are," you say with cold sarcasm. •• What do you want?" "Oh, muffin." "Well,, lie still and go to sleep, then." "I isn't s'eepy, papa." "Well, I am, your man." "Is you? I isn't—not a bit. Say, papa, papa T" "Well ? " "If you was rich, what would you buy me?" "I don't know—go to sleep." "Wouldn't' you buy me nuffin ?" "I guess se—now you—" "What, papa ? " Well, a steam-engine may be; now, go right to sleep." "With a bell that would ring. papa ?" " Yes, yes; now you—" "And would the wheels go wound, papa?" "Oh, yes (yawning.) Shut your eyes now, and— —" "And would it go choo, choo, choo, papa?" "Yes, yes; now go to sleep!" "Say, papa." No answer. "Papa!" "Well, what now?" "Is you 'f'aid of the dark?" "No" (drowsily). "I isn't either, papa." '6 Well ?" "If I was wich, I'd buy you somefin." "Would you?" •• Yes, I'd buy you some ice cweam and some chocolum drops, and a toof brush and panties wiv bwaid on like mine, and a candy wooster, and—" e That will do. You must go to sleep, now." Silence for half a second; then—" Papa—papa!" " what flow?" "I want a jink." "No you don't." "I do, papa." Experience has taught you that there will be no peace until you have brought the " jink," and you scurry out to the bath-room in the dark for it, knocking your shins against everything in the room as you go. "Now, I don't want to hear another word from you to- night," yOu say, as he gulps down a mouthful of the water he didn't want. Two minutes later he says: "Papa?" "See here, lad.die, papa will have to punish you if—" "I can sea 'dog,' papa." "Welt, nobody wants to hear you spell it at two o'clock in the morning." " dog; is that right?" "No, it isn't; but nobody cares if—" "Then it's 'd-o-g,' isn't it ?" " Yes, yes; now you lie right down and go to sleep instantly !" "Then be a good boy, won't I papa?" " Yes ; you'll be the best boy on earth. Good night, dearie." "Papa!" Well, well! What now ?" "Is I your little boy ?" "Yes, yes; of course."" home mans haven't got any little boys; but you have, haven't you ?" "Yes.' Don't you wish you had two, free, nine, 'leben, twenty. six, ninety-ten. free-hundred little boys ?" The mere possibility of such a remote and contingent calamity so paralyses you, that you lie speechless for ten minutes, during which you hear a yawn or two in the little bed by your side, a little figure rolls over three or four times, a pair of heels fly into the air once or twice, a warm, moist little hand reaches out and touches your face to make sure that you are there, and the boy is asleep, with his heels where his head ought to be.—J. L. Barbour, in Puck,

BY, HENRY YATES. SCENE: Country loom-house, morning after a beef night. Handloom weaver engaged in rectifying his pattern. (Enter Old Thatcher). " Wod ! At id oready, Tummus ? Well, theaw art a keen 'un, as heaw 'tis. Aw'm beawn to do nooan misel' if aw've to carry on like theaw'rt dooin' . Whey, tha's getten thi loom upside deawn nearly—wheer arta weyvin'?" "Hello, Thatcher! Well, aw wanted somebry to turn up, for aw'm nearly maddlet, aw am, wod wi' one thing an' another. Does ta know wod aw've bin doom'? Aw've bin treydin' wrong; aw thowt aw wer at th' Unicorn ageon an' dooin' one o' mi steps, an' aw danced that herd among th' troddles whol aw've brewt a new pattron eawt. Eh me I But it's a pattrou as aw darned tek to th' ware- heawse, an' sooa aw've to pick id eawt ageon. Dear, dear, but it's herd werk this mornin' wi' mi throoat like a stove-pipe an' nowt to cool id wi' Hes ta hed a hair o' th' owd dog yet?" "Nowe. Heaw mon we manage id?" "Nay, aw thowt theate'd ha' browt some leet wi' tha ; aw darn'd ax th' owd cup-an'-saucer polisher, —hon's bin gooin' mad this mornin'—plump mad."

, " Heaw's ihad ? " "Thew'll remember aw took t' briskut yestemeet ; well, aw co'd at Owd Billy-go-Deeper's on mi way hnoam, an' Owd Neversweat said he'd stan' a bit of a fry eawt of his pooak, sooa we clubb'd together for a two o' three onions to mek id tasty, an'id wor tasty, for aw relished id g,radely weel, and landed hooana swaggerin'." " Wod did yo're ..kilse think abeawt t' briskut?" " Briskut ? Well, nod much, for Owd Never- sweat bed fried id o, an' then filled mi pooak wi' lumps o' wood an'tstooan; ithwer thad as lies med eawr Aisle so crabb'd this mornin', an' no wonder, for boo's fond of a sooap o' broth, an' we com'd mek 'em eawt o't' stuff as aw browt hooam." "Whey, Tummus, theaw's bad luck wi' them beef fleets; id wor bud last May as theaw leet thad piece o' stakin' beef be swapped for a two or three rubbin' stooans an' owd fryin'-pon top wi' one o' t' gipsies." "Tha'rt reet ; but aw'm beawn to drop id. . . . Eh! aw wish aw'd ne'er learned step-dancin' ; it's browt me into mony a scrape. Th' owd squire went deawn t' loyn a bit sin', an' aw wer thad moythert I wi' dancin' on t' troddles whol aw forgeet to poo mi toppin', sooa th fat'll be i'tif fire abeawt thad ; an' if aw hevn'd to flit aw's get i no moor fro' th' ho'. . . , . Aw tell tha wod we con do?" Wod ?" "Owd Black Dick lies a lot o' rapput-skins as we con sell, an' eawr Ailse is gooin' to a berryin' this afternoon, at Daisy Fowd Aw con tee. to a bit to throw her off t' scent—eh F" " Capital! "Come reawnd in a bit, an' if boo's off, aw'll put thad Gereen plant eawtside for a bit o' sun—id mat as wed l hey a bitlas us, wod ?" " Grand" (goes of singing)— Derk fleets bring mornin's, tho' often cloudy, An' grief brings pleasure, an' sometimes pain ; An' wherever sweets are comes the chokin' bitters, As sure as sunshine ever follows rain: Poor toil-worn mortals always find their pleasures Cut short with something, either love or strife ; But sleep surrounds us with its soothing mantle, Thus we bravely fight with all the ills of life!

Owd Dicky wor a rovin' blade, As ever swept a scythe, 0; But he hed a ill-tongue'd nag,gin' wife,— Singin hey ! the day is blithe, 0; Owd rantin' Nan coom hooam one day, As Dick wer mekkin' t' dinner, An' ther' wor owd varra Nick to pay, floo's a weary, weary sinner— For hoo'l never mend o' this side t' grave, Except Dick gets a paten', To tee hissel to t' sittin'-tree, An' sell his wife to Satan. 14 . Aw wonder whether Owd Ailse hes gone to yon hillin-up do set . . . By th' mass, but ml throttle's some are dry—aw could lick a berm-tub eawt just neaw . . . . Aw'll gooa an' see if Tummus an' Black Dick's shapin' ; if you Gereen's eawtside we're reet ; here's off! Phew Yon's Quaite Ruchut comin'!" "Good morning, Thatcher; you'll have yourniece up at the warehouse in good time to-morrow—it's to be in Bolton by night." " Aw'll try an' do mi' best, Mr. Ruchut,-but it's a awfully plaauey patron yo' know; aw'm gooin' to see if Tummus at t' green yen's a spare ceawntin' glass for me, for aw've lost mine." " Lost it, or pawned it ?" Well, Owd Billy-go-Deeper's hed howd on't a time or two, but—" "But don't tell another Be—good mornin'." 44 . Phew, Owd Ruchut's alive this mornin' ; aw wonder if he's heeard owt abeawt t' beef fleet. We morn'd stop long at t' Unicorn; we mun ged yon pieces eawt as heawt t' throttles gooas on." _ _ .

No sooner had Thatcher taken leave of his employer than a man we'd him on horseback, and, coming in view of old Tummus, the weaver, a little farther up the lane, the equestrian accosted him : Do you know me?" " Aw know t' voice, but aw've forgotten t' face." "I'm Doctor Bornham, and you're Thatcher?" "Wod ? It's nooan thee as went to Califony abeawt thirty yer sin', is id?" yes."

"Whey, theow brewt me i th' world !" " Yes, and all of your brothers—you were all lads if I mistake not ?" "Tha'rt reet." "110 w many of you are there now?" "There's four onus, an eawr Mark." "Four and your brother Mark—why, is he not one r "Oh, Oh, 0-0-0 ! Whey, hee'R nooan reet ! " Well done, Thatcher ! You're not a teetotaller now, are you ?" " Fooarc'd med'cine's good for mad dogs." "Come along then, and we'll see what the Unicorn can do for us." And away they went, Thatcher and Tummus, Black Dick, and the returned doctor, up the "loyn" from the village, which lay as if asleep in the noon- day sun, past hedgerows that were fast donning their sweet-scented blossoms, where the sylvan choristers vied with each other in making the landscape perfect with their burdens of song, and where the waggoner was alternately singing and talking to his horses as he jogged through the deep ruts with his load of grain to the farm on the height, where the lambs are frisking in a very ecstacy of life, up to the village in which the old- time custom of a beef-night had been observed the night before, and we will enter with them the portal of that hotel, whose walls, could they only speak, would repeat many an eulogism which has , been passed over deceased members of the hamlet,' which would have been voted rank flattery had , they been uttered whilst the subjects had been in the flesh. Here we are. The cow's head and otker etceteras from which the beef had been cut the night before, has gone to the copper, and is giving forth the grateful smell which now assails us, and soon will be upon the table in steaming mugs of broth for those who desire to partake of it, and there will be
THE EXAMINER, SATILRDAY, FEBRUARY 1. 1890.

few who will turn their noses up at it, 'except those I who have spent their" shekels," and cannot therez tore put in an appearance very well at•such a feast with an empty pocket. Such, indeed, was the posi- tion of Thatcher and Tummus when the latter danced a hornpipe upon the treadles, and before the happy inspiration of the rabbit skins had suggested itself to them, and before the happy appearance of th

10 doctor had refreshed their sight. Here we will leave them enjoying their homely songs and humble fare, with the remark that persons who maintain that the simple villagers are solving wild oats, might well afford to look upon their conduct more charitably did they but consider that such innocent gatherings as those are long remem- bered by the actors themselves, and that they serve to lighten by their memories an existence that would be otherwise dull indeed.
A LONDON MURDER.

Thomas Neal, a bricklayer,was charged at the Clerken- well Police Court, on Wednesday, with murdering his wife at Islington on Tuesday morning by cutting her throat. The landlady deposed that she saw the deceased run out of the house bleeding, followed by the prisoner. The police stated that a blood-stained knife was found on him. Prisoner was remanded.

div.head: "DON'T PUBLISH MY NAME."
div.p: "DON'T PUBLISH MY NAME."

Heiv is a question for the reader to answer : Why do some people take delight and pride in seeing their names in print, while others shrink from it as though it were a sort of disgrace ? That is, the mere publicity ; we do not refer to publicity because of any wrong act. Ex- perience further shows that where Dne person is willing to have his name published even where it would do I good, ten hesitate and at last refuse. A striking illustration of this now occurs to ns. The proprietors of the most popular and useful article known to the British public are daily in the receipt of letters from all parts of the country commending it in the strongest and warm- est terms, but almost invariably ending with these words, " Don't publish my name!" Other letters come from vendors and dealers, who themselves certify to the character and standing of their customers, but inform the proprietors that no name are to be used. For example : Mr. George Hickley, Chemist, 101, Church-street, Brighton, writes: "The verbal testimony furnished daily by my customers who have been benefited by Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup would fill a volume. One says that during his residence in Brooklyn (U.S.A.), he caught cold, and had a violent cough. Using Mother ' Seigel's Curative Syrup one week he was able to under- take a voyage to England." Mr. 3. H. Evans, Medical Hall, Market Cross, Lymm, Cheshire, says: "On Friday night last an old lady who had been ailing for years, spoke in rapturous terms of the benefit she had derived from Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, but said she would rather not have her name published." Mr. E. Howard, 184, Old Kent Road, London, writcs : "My customers speak in the highest terms of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, but do not want to appear in print. A neighbour who keeps an eating-house, says it has cured him of indigestion and dyspepsia." _ .

Laing, 101, Commercial Street, Lerwick, Shetland, says: "My customers say that Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup is the only medicine that does them any good, but seem to be afraid of having their names in print. Yet my sales have doubled the past year." Mr. James Woods, Viewing Rendall, Orkney, says: "My customers of en speak of the good done them by Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and want others to know it, but ask me not to publish their names, but to have people write to them." Mr. Matthew Crewdson, 25, King-st., Ulverston, in- forms us "that the sales of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup are astonishing. The demand for it never falls away, and all the people praise it. A farmer, who asks ma to withhold his hame, said it had curpd him of a severe stomach disease after all the medical men had failed."

Mr. H. Wilson, Drug Hall, Holyhead, writes :—" I re- ' commend Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup before any medicine in my shop. My customers think as highly of it as I do, but object to having their names appear in any book or newspaper. lam ready to endorse it with my own name anywhere in the world." Mr. R. Needham, Leeds, writes: "One of my cus- tomers told me her husband had derived more benefit from a single dose of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup than from all the medicine prescribed by two doctors who had previously attended him. She requests nee not to give her name."

Mr. F. J. Neade, Terenure-road., Rathgar, writes: "I know many ctases of people relieved and cured by Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, but who object to the facts being made public. There is one exception : "Mr. Hynes, of 2, Ratitgar-square, had long suffered from a tomach affection, which neither I nor three doctors could, relieve him of. One bottle of the Syrup completely ure d him."

Mr. J. Cocks, Manager. 7, Westgate-st., Ipswich, writes: "A customer of ours, a farmer, whose name I do not feel at liberty 'to disclose, was very ill about three years ago, with indigestion and liver complaint. At times he was confined to his bed. The local doctor treated him for several months without good result. Then he came to town, and was trested for a long !rime by a leading physician, to wl4om he paid ten pounds, but was no better. To another doctor he paid nine pounds, all for nothing. An acquaintance said, Why don't you try MotherSeigel's Curative Syrup ?' The farmer laughed as if it were a joke. His friend iwisted, ani at last the farmer yielded, and tried it. A few doses gave him marked relief, and in a few weeks he was entirely well. I know the case personally, and also all the doctors alluded to. This farmer is often in my shop, and recqm- mends Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup to everybody. I know other cases like it, but people say they don't like to have their names mentioned." From these facts we may judge how vast an army of persens are indebted to this remedy for life and health, besides the few who are willing their names should appear in the public prints.

div.head: TIIE GALES.
div.p: TIIE GALES.

MANY WRECKS AND GREAT LOSS OF Lug. The crew of the coal beat, Sarah Mills, of Aber- deen, when northward of Montrose, on Saturday morning filled and foundered, and her hands, four in number, were drowned. The Irex, of Greenock, voyaging from Glasgow to Rio Janeiro, stranded on Saturday night near the Needles. An attempt was made to launch a boat, but unsuccessfully, and the captain and the mate perished. The vessel was soon a wreck, but the crew clung to the „rigging, and remained there all night. A lifeboat tried to reach the ship, but in vain. By means of a hawser, how- ever, several men were rescued, but others were drowned. The shipping disasters on various parts of the coast have been numerous, and inward and outbound vessels have had fearful experiences, being swept by huge seas that have done much personal injury and great damage to craft. One of the most extraordinary perils of the sea recorded is that of the steamer Yorkshire, which arrived in the Mersey on Sunday from Boston. Three of her crew were blown off the foreyard into the sea, and two of the men were drowned. Inland great damage has been done by floods, particularly in the Midlands and the North. A telegram from Lloyd's signal station at Dover, timed noon, Monday, reports as follows : Steamer Paris, of Newhaven, from Dieppe for Newhaven, has arrived le the bay disabled, and steaming slowly. The Paris had damaged her starboard paddle wheel. She consequently drifted, and when off Cape Grisnez, on Sunday, it was feared she would go ashore, but by the exertions of the captain she was got out into the open channel again. The passengers state they experienced very severe weather, but the greatest order was maintained on board, where they had every comfort. The anchor steamer Anchoria has arrived at New York, and reports having had her decks swept. Numerous shipping casualties are reported around the coast, but the crews were rescued. A Freshwater Bay correspondent says that up to ten o'clock on Sunday night 24 hands had been brought ashore from the stranded ship hex in Totland Bay, and there was every chance of the remaining six survivors being rescued. The Hamburg-American Company's steamer Servia, from Hamburg for New York arrived at Southampton, at 2 p.m. on Sunday, with her shaft cracked. SAFETY OF THE MANITOBAN. A Greenock correspondent writes :—The Allan Line steamer Manitoban, which was due at Greenock on the 20th inst., from Boston, reached that port safely on Mon- day. The captain reports that he was hove to for three days in a north-west cyclone. The after decks were swept, the saloon and deck cabins flooded, and over 300 head of cattle killed. The vessel received other damage, but no personal injury is reported. LOSS OF A_STEAMER AND 400 PASSENGDRS.

On October 25 the steamer Duburg, a vessel of 1,097 tons burden, which had for some years been engaged in the china trade, left Singapore for Amoy, via Hongkong, with 400 Chinese on board, who were returning home from the Straits Settlements, and has not been heard of since. It was thought she might have gone ashore on one of the numerous rears and islands of the China SO and the steamer Ashington was commissioned to search for her, but no trace of the Duburg or her passengers was found, and all hope has therefore been now aban- doned. Somefloating bundles of rattans observed by vessels between Singapore and Honkong am supposed to have belonged to the ill-fated vessel.
LOSS OF A BRITISH SIT' AIND 30 LIVES.

A:London correspondent received the following tele- grame from Lloyd's, sent by their Amsterdam agent, on Monday morning :—The British ship Loch Moidart, from Iquique for Hamburg, has gone ashore at Callandsoog, and is a tiStal wreck, Thirty of the crewe were drowned. The Loch Moidart was an iron ship of 2,000 tons register, owned by the General Shipping Company, Glasgow. The owners of the Loch Moidart have received con- firmation of the loss of the vessel. She had 32 men on board, of whom all but two are believed to have perished. The captain was W. B. Andrews, of London, and the crew was shipped at Melbourne, except four, who were shipped at l'isagua.

div.head: GALLANT RESCUE BY POLICEMEN.
div.p: GALLANT RESCUE BY POLICEMEN.

A plucky rescue has just been effected by two mem- bers of the Bristol Water Poli es, Sergeant Clarke and Constable Humphries, who in a boat forced their way through the swollen torrent of the covered channel of the river, beneath the streets of the city, and reached a workman, named Charles Williams, who had fallen through a man-hole in the centre of the city. His escape was entirely due to his finding an old shoot, to which he clung till rescued.
SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR
SHEFFIELD. TW 0 MEN KILLED.

Early yesterday morning, the bodies of two Men named William Williamson and James Till were found on the railway at Woodhouse Mills, near Sheffield, in a frightfully mangled condition. The two men who resided in Brighton, in Derbyshire, had been engaged by the Midland Railway Company in connection with the making of additional sidings near Woodhouse Mills Station, and it is supposed that while proceeding to their work they were knocked down by a passing train.

THE NATIONAL GYMNASTIC • CHAMPIONSHIP. WARRINGTON BEAT EXETER HALL. The tie between the Warrington and Exeter Hall (London) Gymnasiums, in the first round for the competition for the National Physical Recreation Society 200 Guineas Challenge Shield, was decided on Saturday evening,- at the Gymnasium of the Exeter Hall Y.M.C.A., at 92, Long=adre, before a goodly number of spectators. The opposing teams were Warrington Gymnasium v. Exeter Hall Gymnasium, and comprised eight members on each side. The competition is the fourth of its kind, the winners last year being a team from Birmingham, who in the final tie defeated Liverpool by the narrow margin of one point. Saturday evening's contest proved a very interesting aihj close one, and , the issue was in the balance right up to the finish. The single bar bell exercises were gone through by both teams m creditable style, but neither obtained the maximym number of marks allowed, which was 96, the nearest approach being 88 by the Warrington men, their opponents comingwithin two points, scoring 86. On the parrellel bars each gave one volunt—ry exerciae, marks being given for the best exhibition of strength, skill, agility, and grace, no one to score more than 12. The London team did .hest at this, Henrick obtaining 11 points, while Barratt, Butters, Hanson, and Owen each scored 10, their aggregate amounting to 74. Warrington, on the other hand, only secured 71 points, G. Vernon and J. Podmore heading the list with 11 points each. The high jump, which was:the third event, proved somewhat tedious, occupying, asit did, close upon an hour. Start- ing at 41t.2in. they progressed until sft. lin. was reached. This proved too much for all but Warren and Nye, who cleared and registered the full number of points allowed. The competition was very keen, and at the finish it was found both teams had scored 67 points. It was in this department that the Exeter Hall representatives did exceedingly well, three of their men clearing sft. Only one point separated the two teams when the last event was commended, but it wai soon apparent that the Wmingtonians could climb the rope, and a close finish was expected. Not until four on each side had made attempts to score a highest pos- sible (12 for three successive plimbs) did the visitors take a lead. This they did #irough the performance of Locker, who managed to negotiate the rope twice, and score eight points, thus placing his side in front: This advantage was maintained by the last three men, who each scored six points to five registered by the Exeter Hall men, and in the result they obtained 48 to their opponents' 43. This gave thein a lead of five on the event, and qualified them for the second round by four points, their total scare being 274 to the London team's 270. Mr. T. Chesterton, Inspector of Physical Training to the London School Board, ably officiated as judge. The following table gives a complete list of points scored by each competitor : •

div.head: RACE ROUND THE WORLD.
div.p: THE RACE ROUND THE WORLD.

Miss Nellie Bly arrived at New York, at four o'clock, on Saturday afternoon, having completed her tour round the world in seventy-two days and a few hours, thus beating her rival, Miss Bisland. who is expected to arrive in the Cunarder Bothnia, this week. She has accomplished the somewhat novel experiment about a week sooner than she anticipated before starting. She was met at the station by a crowd of over 50,000 per- sons, who gave her a great ovation, and greeted with much applause a short speech delivered by the plucky young lady.
MR. GLADSTONE AND THE RECENT BOY- COTTING CASE.

A postcard has been received from Mr. Gladstone by a Mah chester correspondent who forwarded him newspaper extracts reporting the conviction of the Salford boy- cotters as conclusive proof boycotting was as illegal in England as in Ireland :—"Sir,—l think the proof, if any, appears to be that a particular offence punishable in Ireland is also punishable in England. But this has never been denied. It iemains true that other acts lawful in England have been made penal in Ireland, to the great discredit of the Ministry and the Parliament.—Yours, faithful and obedient, W. E. GLADSTONE."

div.head: BUYING OUT OF IRISH LANDLORDS, • MASS MEETING IN LONDON.
div.p: THE BUYING OUT OF IRISH LAND- LORDS, • MASS MEETING IN LONDON.

A mass meeting to protest against the buying out of Irish landlords at the expense of the British taxpayer was held, in St. James's Hall, London, on Tuesday night. Mr. William Saunders presided, Pitofessor Stuart, M.P., move 4 a resolutiou condemning any scheme of land pur- chase which would entail a risk to the British taxpayer for the benefit of Irish landlords. Mr. Jaitin Burns seconded, and said private property in lana was an anomaly. an injustice, and an unmitigated curse to the community. Mr. Michael Davitt said they were met to denounce a scheme which, under the pretence of settling the agrarian ills of Ireland, Meant the perpetuation of landlordism at the expense of the British taxpayer. He affirmed that the Ashbourne Act was merely an Irish landlord relief Act, which would increase the miseries inflicted by landlordism in Ireland. The proposal was not an honest attempt to settle the question, but to multiply landowners in Ireland in order to strengthen the forces of Conservatism and to obstruct the progress of reform. The question was an international one.— The resolution was carried with enthusiasm.

div.head: DRUNKEN WOMAN'S DEATH.
div.p: A DRUNKEN WOMAN'S DEATH.
Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner for South-West Lanca- shire, on Saturday morning held a Court at the Police Station, to inquire into the circumstances of . . .

the death of Harriet •Bailey, wife of Thomas Bailey, chemical labourer, of Litton's-row, Mersey-street. —Joseph Bailey, son of the deceased, said that when he returned from his work on Saturday, the 18th inst., he found his mother drunk. Re left the house, and did not return until night, when he noticed that his mother had a black eye, and that her face was burnt. His father was not in the house. Witness had brought drink for his mother on many occasions, and had pledged things to obtain it: He had heard his father complain of her drunken habits.—Sarah Ann Bailey, daughter of the de- ceased, said that on the Saturday in question, her father left the house early in the morning to go to his work. Her mother had been drinking heavily on the previous night, and when witness came home from her work at 2.30 on Saturday the deceased was lying on the sofa still very drunk. Wirness's father came home about , three o'clock, and as deceased refused to get his dinner; out of the oven, angry words passed between them, the result being that her father struck the deceased with the hack of his hand, and knocked her to the floor. Her father was vexed at finding his wife drunk, he being a sober man. Later in the day her mother rolled off the sofa, with her face against the bars of the fire. De- ceased continued to drink heavily on the following Sun- day, Monday, and Tuesday, and scarcely ate anything. She, however' Aeemed to be in her usual health on retir- ing to bed on Wednesday night. Her father awoke wit- ness about 2.15 on Thursday morning, and said that he had found deceased dead in bed.—Dr. Smith deposed that he had made a post-mortem examination of the body, and found that death was probably due to an epileptic fit, brought on by excessive drinking. Theblow struck by the husband had nothing to do with the death —A verdict in accordance with the medical evi- dence was returned.
DROWNING CASE AT WARRINGTON.
THE DANGER OF HOWLEY BROOK.,

On Thursday morning, at the Warrington Bride- well, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner of South-West Lancashire, held an inquiry considering the death of John Ernest Whitlow, eight years of age, son of Joseph Whitlow, butcher, 30 Fennel-a, who was on Tuesday drowned in Howley Brook. The father said the deceased left home on Tuesday afternoon to go to school. Witness afterwards heard that he had been drowned, and identified the body when it was found. Witness could not say whether the bridge from which the deceased fell was or was not private property, but the brook was very open and ' dangerous. It was net fit for a grown-up christian to go past, not to speak of a child. It was no good talking about his child now, but he should like something to be done for the sake of other chil- dren. There were always a deal of children playing there, and there was noting to stop them going straight from the school to the brook. A boy named John Hardman said that on the day in question he was playing with the deceased near the brook. The deceased jumped on to a hillock in the stream, and then fell into the water. Witness and some other boys tried to get him out, but could not, as the "fresh " was too strong and carried him away.—A witness named Shaw deposed to grappling for and re- covering the body of the deceased.—A discussion then followed as to the state of Howley Bro4k, in which the Coroner, Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (deputy-town clerk), Mr. Longdin (borough i surveyor), Mr. H. Fairclough, and several jurymen took part.—me Coroner said that on the occasion of his holding a previous inquest, he under- stood that the Corporation were going to do something. —Mr. Longdin said that ever since the occasion referred to they had been trying to get the matter settled. No matter what the Corporation might do, if the land out- side the borough, winch was not under their control, re- mained in the same condition as at present, no benefit would result. In 1881 he made a report on the subject, and a meeting of the owners of the property in the district was held, but they did not come to terms with the Corporation. At the present time there was an Extension Bill before Parlia- ment, which would take in the Twice Brook and then the matter could be remedied. The matter was coming up again, on Monday, before a committee, to see if the danger could be done away with. —Mr. Whittle: It is really a private watercourse.—Mr. Fairclough said it was , not a brook, but a sewer. It was also a storm overflow far the town sewers.—The Coroner said he looked at the , matter from the point of view of the protection of life ; it seemed to him that the brook was dangerous to life.— . A Juryman said that he was on the jury when the other boy was drowned. He thought that at that time the Borough Surveyor showed that if the Corpor- ation had been responsible the recommendation of the jury would have been carried out; there seemed to be various parties interested in the matter, and difficulties got in the way. He thought that certainly something should be done to protect the brook. He thought that if the Corporation had power they shoold force the parties concerned to take steps to prevent any further accidents of this kind.—The Cor- oner agreed that it was a very dangerous thing that the brook should run through the borough, and that the lives of the people, especially of children, should be en- dangered in consequence of its unprotected state. The jury had not to deal with the civil liability of any per- son, and they were not sitting as arbitrators ; their only duty was to say whether the death was accidental, or whether some one was criminally responsible for it. If the , Corporation could not carry out the reform, he did not see how the jury could do it. The recommendation of the previousjury was that the brook be covered over. They recommended that the Corporation should remedy the defect. Perhaps in due course the Corporation would intimate how many more lives they wanted wasting before steps were taken.—ln answer to a juryman the Coroner said that he thought the discussion would be sufficient without again adding a rider to the verdict.— Mr. Whittle said that he would bring the opinions expressed by the jury before the Town Council, and a verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

div.head: CATHERINE'S MISTAKE,
div.p: CATHERINE'S MISTAKE,
A SECRET FOR YEARS

CHAFFEE, L. "HE COMETH NOT." CHTMATMAS morning broke, with a raw, cold mist dis- guising it. The bare trees were beaded over with the damp, and those in the distance looked grey and tm- defined as the hills. The country Toads were broken up by the previous frosts, and were now...scarcely passable. Still, Catherine, on foot, and through the cold morning air, journeyed patiently along them. She had risen at six o'clock, to set out for Redfern

Church; and now, at eight precisely, the little square tower mime in view, buried among the tall elms and pines in the corner of the park. She did not look much like a bride, poor thing as, weary and travel-stained, she entered the little gate of the churchyard. Her black garments imparted a sad and sombre aspect to her figure, and her unveiled _ .

face was not that of a joyful bride. Many and mournful thoughts had filled her heart during that long, solitary walk. Her reflections turned sadly on the character of the man who was thus strangely about to become her husband for the second time. True, she loved him dearly, or, rather, the old love, which had never wholly died out of her heart, had revived again in youthful vigour, and fastened itself passionately about him. True; but the man she h..id loved was not in the same degree Worthy of that love now. She thought of him in his youth and freshness, in his purity of soul and rectitude of heart; then as he was now—the fair promise gone, the full ripeness of sin upon him; is lonely life, blighted by the evil be himself had wrought; his forsaken home, his dead son and ungrateful daughter—and then infinite pity filled her heart, as she thought of these things, and his yearning for something better, the something better which she might bring to his repentant heart —the hope of a purer and holier life. And then she said— "For this I marry him—for this, and this only. God, help me in my work! God help me in my teaching!" The hand of the clock was pointing five minutes beyond the hour. Strange that the church doors should not be open, nor the bridegroom looking out, She walked all round the graveyard, but not a sound Was there beside her own footfall, and no living creature in sight. Half-past eight, and still no came. -- Her feet were very cold and wet, her face was blanched, and her hands trembled as she sat down at last on the rails of a little tomb beneath a yew tree, to watch the face of the clock and the pathway across the park. Never, in all the after years of her life, did that forlorn woman forget those hours of her life— the e two hours she sat and watched for a face that never appeared, a step that never stirred the dead leaves on the ground. If you, reader, know what it is to wait at the tryst- lug-place, and wait in vain, to you I need not recount her silent agony of mind, her wretched fears, her tears, too deep down in their fount to flow; nor how she envied the peer little birds their joyous flight, the grazing sheep in the park their happy unconscious- Bess ; how, at last, she feared to lift her eyes to the remorseless clock, whose hand would steal the precious moments from her sight.; how her ears were rendered so acute that she heard the far-off flutter of a leaf to the ground, and thought, with a start, " He 005158 1" No ; silence still; the leaf has settled dawn—the path is empty. Watch again. A robin perched in a hawthorn bush, quite near, suddenly burst forth into sons—a nlaintiye, sweet little song, but wintry and chill as the scene around —filled with fitful gusts of melancholy, and then dying away in a sort of lingering, sweet despair. It was a strange, joyless song, that of the robin, and when it was ended, and the little creature gone, Catherine's tears fell, for its sadness had gone straight to her heart, and melted its hardness. Then she rose, and thought, "Where shall I go? The roof and chimneys of Redfern rose high above the tree-tops. She cast a wistful glance that way, then bent her steps toward them. She knew, as she went, the master was not there; she felt that he could not be in that house alive, and she waiting hopelessly in the churchyard. There was an air of strange solitude about the place. No signs of busy life were visible; not a chimney of all the great stacks sent up a curl of smoke through the foggy air. The shutters, too, were all closed, and the hall door locked. She rang the great house bell, and its deep-sounding reverberation sent all the rooks fluttering from their roosts in the elms with a dismal croaking. She waited some time on the steps, and then the bolts within were shot back, the door opened, and Domingo's black face looked out. "Lora, its Misay Wace! Blest! Well, Fee berry glad to see you again, missy, berry glad. Massa not come home since last night. Missy Cle not 't home, Massa Maxall not 't home—no one 't home 'cept me and the rest ob 'em."

And then Domingo shuffled along, and opened the door of the library for her to enter. The shutters were closed, and there was no fire in the grate, for whisia inadvertency Domingo apologised, sivinkthe -- servants were all in bed except himself. " (it, oey like, missy, when you go. I rout 'orti up, wyw though, lazy debils! You seen mama oh late?* "When did you see him last?" ft Yesterday night he come home, but rode off agin d'reetly ; not seen him since, missy. I come light up de tire prensly; wake up dem debils first." But Domingo had been gone a very few minutes I Wore he returned, with his black face many shades whiter, and trembling all over. "Oh, missy! my poor dear massa—roy poor dear ' massa! " What is it, Domingo?" she cried, starting up; " what is it ?" "0 Lor ! 0 Lor! his horse—dat are horse he rode last night—is waiting at the stable gates, but no mama!" And he rushed away, wailing, miserably. Catherine was lying insensible on the floor. It was a long time before her senses returned, and then it was the kind face of Madame Bernstein that first greeted her dizzy sight, and Lina, kneeling at her was gently chafing her stone-cold hands with her own tiny ones. "Catherine, my poor Catherine! are you better now? There is no one here, no one save Lina, to see that I know and love you. Poor thing! what a hard fate is yours." She led, almost lifted, the fainting cruature to a sofa, and then pillowed her head on her stout arm, and told Linn to go and get spme wine and water immediately. Line ran, and when the door had closed on her, madame whispered— " You need not mind the child, Catherine, she knows cal—it must all come to light now—and the --" But the listener opened her white lips, and gasped out A name— Mr. Ingestre ?" Her imploring eyes said the rest. _ "

"Well, my dear, it is a sad thing," was the re- spouse ; "hut, then, if gentlemen will behave like felons, they muq, expect a felon's punishment. Who would have thought that, after all these years going by, it should come to light! Some one is a traitor. Catherine. and for my- part, I suspect that black servant Georgo brought with him from Jamaica, and tin, ward together, have made out this and that, until they have made up a ease against him. I fear things look very black, my dear. You know he did marry you, although be denied it so wickely afterwards: and then he certainly has married another lady whib, you were alive, and brought up his children ss legitimate. What a mercy that fine young msa never lived to know it !—and the poor girl, too. Oh, my dear, George is a very heartless and wicked reau! Poor Catherine's astonishment at hearing this was very great she could only ask one thing—. 117 ere was lie?" tt My dear, have you not he)rd ? Then what have they been frightening you with? My child! George ingestre is hi St. David's Gaol, arrested on the charge of bigamy." . The bearer did not faint again; she opened her large eyes with wonder and amazement, and said— "I do not (lu4te comprehend. Will you tell me, clear madame ?" "As far as I can hear, Catherine (for Mr. Ingram brousdit the news this morningl, some one has found . out that he married you before he married his last "But. the marriage with me," she gasped, "was not a legal one. I showed you the letter in which he ' said so, in Jamaica. You saw that letter? " "Certainty, I remember but too well; but I sup- pose it was a marriage after all, and some one is trying to prove it so. I must tay I never supposed George Ross capable of such a piece of villany; but I there's no saying what men will do when they an tempted. There are some strange things coining to light, my poor Catherine—we must be prepsred. Oh, here is Dina." But Catherine had sunk back, unconscious om'e more.

A114F.5T OF THE VICTIM'S TWO SONS.

• Late on Saturday night a shocking murder was perpe- trated on the highway bet Ween Crewe and a ,village -known as The Hough, some three miles distant, the victim beim,. Richard Davies, a tailor, aged 51. Davies was very well off,- having considerable property in I 'Crewe. He kept an extensive tailor and draper's estab- lishment, in Victoria-street, where he stayed a great deal, but Went once or twice a week to The Hough, Where he had a residence, and where his wife and family reside. He invariably drove home at week ends, and Vent Sunday with his wife and children, -of whom he had nine. On Saturday night the murdered man and Ills son, George Davies, aged 16, who is employed in his father's shop, left Crewe about 11 o'clock, in their pony "rali• Mr. Davies was driving, and the night was extremely dark. After passing through Gresty the roads may be described as winding country lanes. Here and there tall trees over-lap the roadway. Mr. Davies and his son appear to have driven the greater part of the • Way home without incident, but just before entering the 'village, and while they were going along a very lonely Place in the road, two men, the son says, jumped out 'of the hedge. The night was so dark that their Agures could not be seen. They laid hold of the pony's head and stopped it. George Davies tried to urge the animal forward by means of a stick, but, being unsuc- tessful, he "got out of the trap. No sooner had ila done this than one of the men at the Pony's head, rushed back to the old man in the vehicle, B, truck him a terrible blow on the head, and dragged 'nal into the road. ,The boy, seeing the attack on his father, endeavoured to make his escape, but the second ruffian, who was at the pony's head, left it and com- menced to chase the boy round the trap. The boy 'lodged him, and the fellow pursued him about 400 yards the road, but finding he could not overtake him, turned back to his companion, who was wrestling with Davies. The boy passed several houses, and ran on to his home, where he got an elder brother and several v, illagers to go back with him. They found Mr. Davies Ong dead at the side of the road, his head being bat- tered out of all recognition. From the state of the road it was evident that there had been a terrible struggle for life. For several yards there were pools' of blood, while great quantities of blood cn the grass and on both sides 01 the road led to the belief that the poor man had endea- voured to escape from his assailants by attempting to 2Vee'p through gaps in the hedget In addition to having head battered in the murdered man had his right thumb cut off, and two fingers on the same hand broken. Ilia body was found several yards from the spot where the first attack was made,while the pony was discovered alone. the side of the road, about 50 yards nearer the village. 'The attack was of a most daring charac- ter, for there are houses within about 200 yards,while the ihurdered man's dwelling is not more than 600 yards svra3'. It was ascertained that Mr. and Mrs. Moses, Market gardeners, from Crewe, drove over the same Vet 10 minutes previously, and they saw no one in the r(lacl ; while the people living near said they did not hear anY cries for help. The motive for the crime is inexpli- cable. The deceased had about £lO when he left Crewe, and there is no doubt his pockets had been rifled, for !vlieri found he had only sixpence. His pocket knife was "Ind lying unopened in the road. Robbery, how- :Vrr, could scarcely have been the sole object, the murderers did not take his watch and chain, *l,ough his watch had been taken out of his pocket. Some of the villagers ascribe the deed to revenge, but the deceased was a quiet man, and it .is not Dc'wn that he had had a quarrel with anyone. It is a rtriewhat singular circumstance, however, that about ul,ree Years ago the murdered man and his son (not e soianho amaanpanied him home on Saturday) were turnirmealong the same road, and they were attacked as nearlyass possible on the same spot. They, however, ,Icanaged to beat off their assailants. On' Sunday the s".,;'eae was the subject of much discussion in Crewe, • _ here the murdered man is well known, and notwith- _l-ancling the rough, boisterous weather large numbers ire visited the scene of the tragedy. Colonel amersley, the Chief Constable of Cheshire, with a 'lumber of detectives, were in the village during the 'lay, and every circumstance that can throw any light „ • :Don the crime is being thOroughly investigated. A 'arrespondetit paid a visit to the village and at the resid- thee of Mr. James Edwards, a local gentleman, had an int erview with the boy, George Davies. The lad seemed terribly depressed on account of the murder of his father, and appeared to think that he himself had had a Zit's-callous escape from a similar fate. He confirmed e statement that as they were driving along in a !eeluded spot two men rushed out and without a word ! 'tanned the pony. It was pitch dark, and their move- ' Ments could not be well observed. When they stopped the momentPouy he got down to see what was the matter.At that t one of the men attacked his father, who was in ile trap,and the other tried to get at him Re dodged round ' the horse and trap, and, watching the opportunity, he 114;1 off as hard as he could up the road, shouting "Help! !" The man followed him some distance, and then ent back. He described the man who followed him .'ac.l wearing dark clothes and a stiff hat. He could not enti!'y the features of either of the men. When he d given the alarm, and his brother and himself and didagers had arrived at the spot where his father lay nothing could be seen of the assailants, who ap- `,"•,a,red from footmarks to have got through the hedge made off in the direction of Crewe railway station. ' 'le lad added that he noticed one of the men had what appeared to be a heavy stiek in his hand. s. Mathews and Travis, however, who examined the rounds of the murdered man, said the injuries on the must have been inflicted by some sharpinstrument. is believed the murderer used a hatchet or hammer. ~.ae Police discovered near the place a heavy rail, which L'a2S covered with blood and hair. This had evidently ;en used to batter in deceased's skull. Deceased waS t ell known in Crewe, where he had carried on business DZ a number of years, and was much respected. It ap- ,tars he had been in the habit of carrying large sums of a4"),,neY from his place of business to his house at Hough, he knowledge of this might have furnished a otive for the commission of the crime. ,kri examination of the trap in which the murdered blood was riding at the time he was attacked shows n b )th wheels and a considerable quantity o blood on the seat and cushions. It is, therefore, evident i_t.tt Mr. Davies must have been struck a fearfablow tTicire he was dragged out of the vehicle. The crime is t;')e subject of considerable . cdmment througholit the triwn, and it is somewhat singular that, although the wnrdered man was undoubtedly robbed, there is a tt!nderfol agreement of opinion that robbery was not ut'enprirue motive the murderers had, in view. It is r allY believed to be revenge arising out of some •rrel the deceased must 'have had with someone. opinion is shared by the sons of the murdered man, in course of conversation declared their belief that „WI. murder was premeditated and planned by somebody Th2,knew the deceased and the neighbourhood intimately. 4ey's of the safe in the murdered man's shop were in"n"LePorted missing, but they were found by the police ii ,71,x On the premises, having been accidentally left o shop. The deceased owned four shops in Crewe in Victoria-st. and two in Ifeath-st.--besides er property. STARTLING DISCOVERY.

i„ TII11"Eii-sATIONAL ARRESTS. tlat—ense excitement continued at Crewe on,VVednes- tet.,llight, in consequence of the arrest of the two sons •e,e"e murdered man. Both youths are well known in c. The elder prisoner, who walked home a distance No4"'ree miles, fails to explain satisfactorily where he s for three hours before the murder. The blood on .61.1" e clothes of both the prisoners is regarded with grave sPiclon. It is stated that Richard, the elder son, had ati4,l differences .with his father regarding money matters, niAti.lie fact that he left the shop on a wet boisterous !° walk home. when he might have Tilden in. .his hill," trap, serves to increase the suspicion against . all," 'rile police are believed to have some extraor 's.t4.vilfence, and further startling developments, with „rhoer arrest, are anticipated. 'list-I,e elder prisoner; Richard Davies, who left on the " of the murder to walk home, wore an overcoat itte gaiters. These have been found at his house, and the c°vered with blood sp/ashes from top to bottom. At 401Irned magisterial examination, several of the °llers' brothers will be called to give evidence. It was a case such yearn:lad not had to investigate in Cheshire for maw have Was very necessary that the police a should lae possible opportunity to make enquiries, ad cove d the result of those inquiries would be the cis- . cri4.3' of the perpetrators ef this most outrage:fits 'day, ' sltnild adjourn the inquiry to a con ien vent sun cessful and he trusted the efforts of the police would be - Su . • ' Perintendent Leah said that at present the mureer • tiollsiejolved in mystery, but he hoped the investio; • Serried' the police would, before the inquest was successful. poti2_ Coroner said if they adjourned until Friday, tie posaiwould have an opportunity to make the tullett • er e inquiry-, and by that time if they did not jour_ anYthing of importance, they could further 2at- With the evidence then presented. • a 15<• rultendent Leah said he hoped they would be ii The .1* Position with evidence on Friday. dale's) son who was present that day acted as a member of the Committee unde4hirn. He was sure they wokld II sprtitiserwith MIL tilfltly and the members of the }mill, "ontlie lost they had austained.-=The Magis- trates' Clerk (Mr. Buckton) said there was no doubt regret would be very great at the loss of Mr. Bleckly's services. The knowledge study and attention which he always brarght to bear on the magisterial affairs and on the county business generallywas of the highest order. He had during his great experience also acquired a very considerable legal knowledge and that, no-doubt, had A great deal to do with the position in which he was placed 1 and the way in which he administered justice especially 'in difficult appeal cases. 011 the occasion to which Col. McCorquodale had alluded he believed there was some very heavy appeal cases in connection with the London and North-Western Railway Co. and other companies anff consideration of which was a great undertaking for one of Mr. Bleckly's age. He was always anxious, ready and willing to attend to the duty he was called upon to perform and very often did so at great inconvenience to himself. He was sure there would be universal sorrow as his loss and that he was no longer able to perform his duties.—Mr. A. Browne remarked that he had been intimately connected with the late Mr. Bleckly for a great number of years especially at the Borough Police Court, at Warrington where he (Mr. Browne) used to act aa clerk under Mr. White. Mr. Sleekly was a constant attender, he never shirked his duties, and he was always one of those magistrates upon whom they could rely with the greatest confidence, equally in decisions of law and on fact. Speaking as one practising at the County Police Court and the Borough Court as well, he could say that he could always rely upon any point argued before Mr.Rleckly being fairly considered and a Very fair decision given by him. The advocatea Who had to appear before him always had great pleasuse in address- ing him, and.in feeling that justice would be done. They would miss him at Warrington both on the county bench arld on thp borough bench, though he had not often ap- peared on the borough bench during the last few years. He had an experience which was not possessed by younger magistrates, and on some matters of import- ance and in certain appeal cases the magistrates would regret the loss of his advice. The community at large would regret his loss as he was always very attentive and patient in the hearing of all cases.—Mr. Knowles (Widnes) supported the views expressed by Mr. Browne. He said he had frequently appeared before the late Mr. Sleekly, and he was a gentleman who always dealt with firmness and kindness to all people who came before him. He was one of those justices whose loss would be keenly felt and he joined with others in expressing sympathy with his I elatives.—The business of the Court was proceeded with. REFERENCES AT ISLINGTON. __

At the CotiVilia..7.;,isTrate.:l76o-u-r-t,--Isliniton, on Mon- day, Mr. W. S. Barrett, the Chairman, said: Before the business of the Court commences, I wish to refer to the loss sustained by the county in the death of Mr. Hairy Bleckly, Chairman of the Quarter Sessions for this divi- sion. For many years Mr. Bleckly was a diligent and able magistrate, devoting much time and attention to the affairs oi the county during the time the county affairs were administered by the magistrates. On the resignation of Lord Derby, Mr. Bleckly was elected to fill the chair at Quarter Sessions, and discharged the duties with marked care and ability. As a business man, Mr, Bleckly was much respected: and I am only expressing the feelings of my colkague and the magis- trates generally when I express the sorrow the county at large has sustained by his loss, and offer our sympathy to the surviving members of his family. MR. BLECKLEY AND THE WARRINGTON CHAMBER

_ OF COMMERCE. The annual meeting of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, which had been fixed for Monday Afternoon, was adjourned for a week as a mark of respect to the deceased, who had been a member of the body for a number of years. The President (Councillor. F. A. Roberts) was in the chair, and there were also present Councillcrs William Pierpoint, William Tinsley, J. H. Fleming, and Frederick Monks, Mr. It. A. Naylor, Mr. John Fairclough, Mr. W. Carson, and the hon. secre- taries (Alderman Davies and Mr. J. L. Tunstall ) The CHAIRMAN said he did not hear of Mr. Bleckly's death till Saturday night, or the chamber would have been officially represented at the funeral ,which wouldl no doubt, however, be attended by some of the member 4 in their individual capacity. He had received a letter from Mr, William Long, who suggested that out of respect to the memory of Mr. Bleckly, who was in a sense the ori- ginator of the Chamber, the annual meeting should be postponed for a week. At tht same time he (the ci- dent) thought it WAS the duty a the chamber to record the loss which had been sustained by the death of Mr. Bleckly. Mr. Bleckly was known all throughout the North of England as a very active and successful busi- ness man, and he was also a most valuable magistrate and member of society. The town of Warrington tad not failed to derive an advantage from Mr. Bleckly's presence in it. He had taken an active part in the affairs of the town, but more especially in the years long past; and he did so with a great deal of success. They knew his value to them as a trader while with regard to the ndotiations they had with the Manchester Ship Canal Company, Mr. Blackly was foremost in premoting the interests of Warrington. They should not separate without passing a vote of condolence with the widow and family. Alderman DAVIES remarked that for many years Mr. Blackly had ably striven to further the interests of the CliamSer, and had pointed out to them also how they could be useful to the manufacturers as a body. Mr. Bleckly and himself had an impression, in the formation of the Chamber, that it was their duty, if possible, to prevent the breaking out of the atrikes that were so frequent at the time. It was the opinion of Mr. Bleckly and himself that a court might be formed to prevent strikes, and that Chambers of Commerce should be a sort of conciliatory court. Be had now to move "That this chamber expresses its deep regret at the ueath of Mr. Henry Bleckly, J.P., one tf its vice-preside.nti and 'members of the Council ; and one who had always taken an able part in all its work, and that the members con- vey to Mrs. Weekly and her family their sympathy in their bereavement," Councillor Monks seconded the motion, and observed that it had never fallen to his lot to have much connection • with Mr. Bleckly, but whenever he had had the pleasure of meeting him he had always been struck with his sympathetic and kindly nature. They had lost a most valuable citizen by the death of Mr. Bleckly, who was alwaysto the front in everything which tended to advance the prosperity of Warrington. As Mayer of Warrington, and as Chairman of the Board of Guardians, he was an example of what a chairman ought to be. He wished they had moremen like Mr. Sleekly to take a share in their public work, and set • an example to younger men as to the manner in which business should be conducted. Mr. Sleekly was always just, and they might correctly speak of his kindly disposition. Ho was no mean poet also, and those who had read his contributions would admit that there was deepthought and a genuine poetical feeling running through them. Mr. Caisson said he could endorse everything Mr. Monks had said. In the multitude of public duties the late Mr. Weekly had to perform, not only for Warring,- ton, but for Lancashire generally, would be pre- pared to 'ehrlorse,the view that his jUdiclal mind, calm judgment, and ready resourceshad never failed to bene- fit the community. It vias astt advantage to possess such a man. He wished more particularly to remind the Chamber of a great advantage they possessed in having had Mr. Bleckly's services at the time of the traders opposition to the Ship Canal Company in the very im- portant question of the water supply. At that time the question was whether they should be deprived of the water which they obtained as manufacturers from the Upper Mersey without any compensation being given them. The indefatigable industry which Mr. Sleekly displayed on that occasion, and the wonderful. way he had of impressing his opponents with the reasonable- ness of the demands of those he represented,. was mani- fest in the most telling way ; so much so, indeed, that in his (the Speaker's) opinion they obtained the advant- age in.the settlenient with the Manchester Ship Canal Company mainly, if not altogether, through the manner in which Mr. Bleckly was able to submit their, cause. The motion was then put to the meeting, and' carried unanimously; and, on the motion of Councillor William Pierpoint, seconded by Councillor Fleming, thts' meeting was adjourned for a week.

„ LOSS OF A BATKIITE AND 16 LITETA Intelligence was received in Queenstown on TueadST night of the total loss of the barque Buteshire and the drowning of her entire crew of 16 hands in the Atlantic during the recent terrible gales. The Buteshire was a vessel of 967 tons, and as on a voyage from Norfolk, Virginia, to the Mediterranean, with a cargo of timber. She was owned in St. John's, New Brunswick.
