f iifos SIDE 'MISRION ROOM Mr. John Watson, Missionary from Runcorn, has been conducting a week's special mission at the Mission room; Moss Side (No. 5 section) during the past week. It has been well attended by the workmen and their wives, and it is believed that it will have a beneficial effect. . ' THE LATE MR. ADAMSON. A meeting ot the Manchester Association of Engineers was held on Saturday night,' at the Grand Hotel, Man- chester. under the presidency of Mr. John West. Before the ordinary business was transacted, the Chairman re- ferred to the death of Mr, Daniel Adamson. The toss of Mr. Adamson, an esteemed member of that society, was one which the whole ce,mniunity deplored. His name had of late years become a household word in the North. His energy, his indomitable pluck in connec- tion with everything he undertook, furnished young men with a fine lesson, In public matters they knew Mr. Adamson as the real author of the Ship Canal. The idea itself was not new, but he was the man who gave a practical turn to it. The meeting at The Towers, at which eleven mayors were present, was the real starting point of the great waterway, which they all believed would confer such an immense boon on the whole dis- trict. In the agitation and Parliamentary struggle which followed that meeting. Mr. Adamson showed what a splendid leader and fighter he was. Six sessions passed before the bill became an Act. He was the one man in the community to fight the battle. The Chair- man concluded by moving a resolution of sympathy with the family of Mr. Adainson. THE WORKS FLOODED: SERIOUS DAMAGE TO PROPERTY. The disastrous gale which visited 'Lancashire and Cheshire. and the neighbouring counties on Sunday caused considerable damage in this district. Fortunately, no serious accidents were reported, but the heavy rain which fell during the whole of Sunday afternoon and at night caused rivers and brooks, particularly on the Cheshire side, to be abnormally swollen. Pursuing the course of the Mersey through the Stretford and Sale districts, there was to be seen on every hand the effect of the storm. The river in many places had overflowed its banks, and the low lying districts for miles around were Submerged to the depth of several feet. Near Heatley and Warburton, and again near Lynam, there were vast expanses of water, where pasture lands and •market gardens are generally to be sear'. The Ship Canal Works did not escape the general submersion. At Thelwall, on that section ot the canal which termi- nates at Latchford Locks, the damage was perhaps more serious than at any other given point. To those who have followed the progress of this gigantic undertak- ing it will be known that the river Mersey twice crossed the route of the canal within a few hundred yards owing to its horseshoe form. The contractor had had, therefore, to divert the stream, and about a mile from Thelwall Railway Station the new course proceeds along the side of the canal for a consider- able distance. The work of diversion is practically complete, and a huge embankment of sand separates the Ship Canal from the river. The cetting for the canal extends about a mile and a half, the excavatious having been carried out in many parts to the required depth. In fact for some distance on the Latchford side the masonry walls have been put in, but nearer Manchester, where the river passes close by, a high embankment of sand has hitherto acted as the main support of the Mersey as it rushes along to the sea. A gap had been left in the embankment for the purpose of putting in , syphons to carry drainage water from the neighbouring, village. Along the side of the proposed canal runs a line , of railway, used by the contractor in the perforerbence of the work, and in the canal cutting were several steam navvies, dozens of railway waggons used in the removal of the spoil, and other plant, including the usual tem- porary lines of railway. This was the condition of, the, canal when the workmen ceased operations on Saturday.. During Sunday night the river had risen several feet, and about six o'clock on Monday morning it overflowed at the temporary gap in the embankment where the Syphons are to be placed. The water, in rushing through, tepidly washed away portions of the soft sand, and Increasing in volumh, it burst away the side of the canal On which the temporary railway is constructed, and flooded the workings. A large quantity of soil was 40149hea late the canal cutting; and the water covered to b. depth of seVeral feet the bottom' of the gully where three steam navvies have for some time been at work. These enormous machines were, of course, stopped. One of the steam navvies, when daylight broke, was found to be under water as far as the foot-plate, and about a score of waggons were submerged to the level of the floors. The water gravitatw along the cutting into the deep cleft in the fe'd 56114289A0• 5, Or so further on, where the foundations for the Latch- ford locks are being formed. The locks were filled with a yellow fluid UD to the level of the main excavation, and the work of the concreters and masons was stopped for the time being. It was very fortunate that the leak was discovered at such an early period of its existence, or the river would in a short time have filled the canal to its own level, and the greatest difficulty would have been experienced in stopping the flow of water, Moreover, great damage would have been done to the works, and much of the plant would have been destroyed. But the minimum of mischief was effected by the flood owing to the prompt and energetic manner in which it was dealt with. All the available men were collected on the spot, and, obeying the in- structions of Mr. Price, the resident engineer, and other Officials who had been summoned to the spot, they threw into the gap scores of bags of cement which hap- pened to be handy, and on the top of them loads of sand were deposited, and so. in the course of a, couple of hours, the satisfactory announcement was made that the leak had been stopped. The gap was then further pro- tected by means of piles, with a backing .af sand, and having thus prevented all further danger from the river, the workmen next Welted their attention to removing the water from the workings. This was a labour of con- siderable magnitude, owing to the fact that the water had extended nearly the whole length of ' the seCtion, and at the leeks it was sixteen feet deep. The steam pumps, ordinarily used, were, however, put to their full power, and were found to be sufficient to reduce the flood water without the aid of additional engines. The result was, that In a very few hours the water in the cutting became appreciably less. The gap made by the torrent from the river left the singular spectacle of a line of rail- way suspended across a chasm about 100 ft. in width. The metals and sleepers hung in mid-air in a kind of loop, and, viewed from the opposite side of the canal, looked exceedingly picturesque, with their high sandy back- ground. Although many of the ordinary workers on the canal were prevented by the disaster from proceeding with the excavations, a considerable number were found occupation in refilling the chasm over which the novel suspension' bridge had been so suddenly formed. The volume of water coming down the river was greater on Monday than it had ever been since the canal works were commenced. In the village of Thelwall the effect of the storm was conspicuously seen near the village school, where the roadway was submerged for a con- siderable' distance to a depth of several feet OFFICIAL VISIT TO THE WORKS. The Consultative committee formed in 1886 "to con- sider the project of the Manchester Ship Canal "paid a visit on Monday to the works at the, Manchester end of the canal. The members of the Committee met at the Pomona docks at half-past nine. After the rain of the past few days the weather was beautifully fine. although the wind was keen and nipping. The intention was to travel along the contractor's railway line as fat a. 4 the docks at Easthani, a distance of 35 miles. Both the Ir- well and the Mersey were in flood, however, and when the flat Cheshire country was reached the railway line,it was discovered,wasunder no less than five feet of water. Near Warburton therefore, progress came to an end. and the party returned. From Pomona the first stage of the journey was to the docks at Salford. Here, as Mr. Leader Williams pointed out, immense progress has been made. The area of the dock space is 114 acres, and of quay space 152 acres, while the length of the quay's is 5f miles.. For two years the work has been in progress, and the engineer gave the assurance that the contractor had " something in hand." In some places the cutting is quite complete, and the walls of red sandstone and concrete are built. The general appearance is one of irregularity, but from the seeming confusion order will in due course be evolved. Leaving Salford, the saloon was taken past the locks and sluices at Mode Wheel, and then a slow progress was made by the river bank. At one point the novel sight was presented of a length of ths canal complete in every way, and filled as it will be two years hence. By someaccident part of the embank- ment which separated the cutting from the river had been broken, and the flood water rushing in had filled it to the river level. At this point the Ship Canal has . a width at the bottom of over 200 feet, whereas the width of the Suez Canal at the bottom is only 120 feet. Passing through Stretford, fears began to be felt of the effects of the flood on the canal works. The water rushed on in a turbulent stream, and one of the temporary bridges' appeared to have escaped disaster very narrowly, for a great quantity of driftwood was piled against the wood- en supports. The fields on the left-hand side of the river tvere flooded, and as far as the eye could reach stretched a great lake. Passing under Brindley's aqueduct at Bar- ton another completed section of the canal was reached, and it was seen that preparations for the locks were pretty forward. There was little to note beyond thisl till the train stopped at Irlam, where further sets of locks and sluices were in progress. From this point to the paper mill at Partington the journey was made with great caution. The Mersey from its junction with the Irw.ell went down with a great swing. There was-an overflow on either bank, and some of the cuttings appeared to have suffered. The railway line runs close to the river bank, and the engine had to plough its way occasionally through a couple of feet of water. Near Warburton there was a final pause. Here the company were assured that the water covering the line was nearly five feet deep. Apart from the fact that

such a depth of water would have put out the boiler fire of the small engine, it was feared that some of the sleilers cf the line might have been washed away, in which case the not improballe disaster was fearol octss:l; train rolling over itito the riirer. Mr. Leader declined tie risk the passage, and relucieintly the, party turned homewards. On tlw way back a pause was made at Mode Wheel to allow the party to.sii4tie7grt basin, big enough to accommodate the finest Atlantic liner, and the elaborate sluices by which the basin is filled and the boats rhised in a few minutes to the height of 15 feet'. There are four such locks in the 35 miles of canal, and so wonderful is the mechanism that only an hour is lost in reaching a level 60 feet higher than that it Liverpool. After passing through the great concrete walls of the look, the company witnessed in a great timber shed the manufacture of the lock gates. The days of iron gates have gone, and we have come back again to wood. The wood that is here being sawn and shaped is the laurel„ and comes from Demerara. It is fashioned in enormous lengths, bolted firmly together. This wood, Mr. Williams told his hearers, is practically imperishable. After the inspection at Mode Wheel, the journey to Pomona was quickly made, and the party separated till Thursday week. During the coming months Mr. Marshall Stephens will periodically take parties of merchants, manufacturers. and traders who are likely to use the canal to see the works. Mr. Stevens is the traffic organiser of the Com- pany, and he is anxious to know what accommodation his future customers will want and to adapt his arrange- ments to the „,eeneral convenience. Very properly, he is anxious that when the canal is opened there shall be ready for it the great volume of trade which if it did not come at first would be bound to come later. Those Yell° are anxious to take advantage of the cheap traffic facili- ties of the canal when it is opened two years hence canntt do better than communicate with Mr. Stephens. The re- port of the late Consultative Committee, the majority 6f the members of which visited the canal works on Thurs- day, may also be commended to the trading public. The advantages of the canal were very clearly pointed out in that report. A short recapitulation may be made of lone or two of the principal facts affecting merchants and traders in this district. An established fact is that cargoes would be carried by vessels from foreign ports to Manchester, Salford, Warrington, and Runcorn at rates of freight and marine insurance not exceeding those charged to Liverpool. This would result in the saving of the charges for bridging some of the principa I articles from a vessel in the Liverpool docks to the rail way station or Bridgewater Canal wharf at Manchester. This sav- ing averages 14s. or 15s, per ton, and would leave to the owner of the cargo, after paying canal rates, at least 50 per cent of the existing charges. On the outward-bound cargo, there would be the same advantage.' The saving on cargoes adjacent to but not actually upon the canal will of course vary with the distance; but it is a broad fact that the canal will be the nearest port for a very large area containing an immense industrial population. The Committee point out the certainity of a great traffic in low-class goods to different poiats on the canal when it is opened far traffic. Of several examples given in proof of this one may be mentioned. The canal being within five miles of the Wigan coalfield, it is certain that , coals from that district for shipment will be sent to the IPartington basin or to Barton. We believe it is also the case that Sir Edward Watkin,formerly one of the staunch- est opponents of the canal scheme, intends to bring South Yorkshire coal—which is eminently suitable for steamers —to the canal, this coal being now almost excluded from such use by reason of the cost of carriage. Coal, again, from South Wales will probably be delivered at Warring- ton. The development of trade indicated by these and similar facts cannotof course take place immediately the canal is opened, but must neeessarily grow naturally' Mleanwhile itis satisfactory that Mr Marshall Steven is. aiteasuring his responsibilities in time. STOCKTON HEATH MISSION. The above room was crowded, on Wednesday even- ing, when the Rev. R. Grimstone. gave a magic lantern entertainment in connect ion with the Band of Hope. It included local views of the Ship Canal. It was most amusing to hear the Ship Canal men who were present, when they recognised their mates in the views.—" Buy your own Cherries" was well received, and " Billys' Rose" was made most interesting by the reading of the beautiful poem by the rev. 'gentleman as the' views were put on the screen. Several melodies were lighted up and heartily sung. At the conclusion a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Orimstone for his kindness, on the motion of Mr. idallow seconded by Mr. Rooks. .The 'same evening, at an early hour, a Childrene entertainment was given at which some comic slides, kindly lent for the occasion by Mr. Vere Davies, were very much en- joyed.

Carleton, Messrs. T. Jones, Heaton, Davies, Ankland. Dobson, J. Houghton, Ratcliffe, Dignum, Mather, Jolley, Gill, Wright, Harrison; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (workhoun motel),

IfOR FIRM The Cumit Said that the repdr6 of 66 Worilhouse master with regard to precautions against fire at the Workhouse, had gone forth in the provincial and Metro- politan as well as the local papers, and the chalrtnan and himself had since been receiving from people who sup- plied that sort of thing plans and specifications of the ways whereby they might meet the supposed difficulty in which they were placed. He found that immediately outside the workhouse gates a fire plug which =lst have been placed there for the purpose of the workhouse. The workhouse master seeing dist this plug was outside the workhouse premises reasonally concluded that it would not be sufficient for the purpoef; but still if the force of water at the plug was adequate,' to suppress a fire out- side it would be adequate for the Ynrkhouse as they had no buildings higher than three storSs and only a few that height. Mr. Sutton also pointed out that in the build- ing of the workhouse every possible prBsaution had been taken to guard against fire. With regard to this sebject the House Ccimmittee re- ported that after careful consideration of the entry in the master's journal they were of opinion that in the event of fire the service of water from the fire plug near the entrance gates would be sufficient for the purposes of the fire brigade, but they approved the suggestion of the master that the Corporation be requested to permit a trial by the fire brigade. They thought also that with an increase of buckets, &c., the present supply on the premises would be sufficient. They recommended, how- ever, as a precaution that inspection be made of the premises with a view to the increase of the means of egress if fire at any time occurred at night.—Mr. RAT. CLIFFE proposed the adoptionof the Committee's minutes. —Mr. HEATON, in seconding the proposal, said heb ‘fieved that on Saturday week they should have the Warrington fire brigade at the workhouse. He added that they were rather better placed with regard to fire than they antici- pated.—The minutes were adopted. SCHOOL FEES. div.head: LATE MR. H. ,BLFKLY.
div.p: THE LATE MR. H. ,BLFKLY.

',built young man of 20, and George Davies, the youth of 1.0 who was with his father when lieldrove home, live with their parents at the Hough, and were both ern- ploy..d by their father to assist him in his business at Crewe. • They were brought before 'the &mull at three o'clock on Wednesday afternoon. the 'only magistrate present hcing Mr. E. Bellyse. The prisoners on being brought into the court %vac allowed to be seated on a bench in front of the dock. Neither of them seemed 'to fully appreciate the fearful position they Were in. Richard sat with his hands in his trouser? pocket se and betrayed little agitation beyond giving occasional !quick glances round the court, towards the door when anyone entered. He was very pale. George Davies was deadly pale, his hair was rough, and he held his hat in his hands and nervously, tvvitched it. On Use entrance ' of the magistrate the prisoners were placed

TRH DOCK, and thert their demeanour through the bearing was similar to what it was while they were seated. Richard listened intently to the evidence of the Superintendent, and at the close, when asked if he had any questions to ask, said in a firm and cool tone that ha. had nothing to ask except that he thonght Superintendent Leah was wrong in witat he said about the length of time he had been home when his brother arrived sayin,g that his father had been stopped. The younger prisoner seemed to take a less intelligent interest in the proceedings, and looked on sullenly. The matter had been kept so quiet that only thirteen persons were present as representing the public, and Richard nodded to one of these whom he apparently recognised as an acquaintance. The Chief Constable, Colonel Hammersley, was present. The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. C. E. Speakman) read the charge against the prisoners as follows :—" That Richard Davies and George Davies, at Basford, on the 25th January. 1890, feloniously, wilfully, and of malice afore- thought did kill and murder one Richard Davies."

SUPERINTENDENT LEAH'S STATEMENT. Superintendent Jesse Leah was then sworn, and de- posed that the deceased, Richard Davies, carried on busi- ness s a clothier, at 85, Victoria-st., Crewe. The two prisoners assisted himn the shop. Some part of the family reside at the shop, and the other part at a small farm at The Hough, and it was the custoio of the de-. ceased to drive home to The Hough on Saturday even- ings, after closing his shop in Crewe. The elder brother, Richard, left the shop at eight o'clock on Satur- day night, to walk home to The Hough. The decased left at 10.30, together with the younger prisoner,George, to drive home in a pony trap. Richard, the elder pri- sener, arrived home first at about eleven o'clock, and in about ten minutes afterwards the younger prisoner ran into the house saying "My father has been stopped on the road in Crewe-lane." They both then appear to have left the house, and gone and called up one or two neigh- bours, including their brother John, who lived near, say- ing their father had been stopped on the road. The brother John went, and about midway in the lane men- tioned, the body of the deceased was found lying by the road side. He then appeared to be dead, and there were some eight or nine severe wounds on the head. I saw the body at four o'clock the next morning (Sunday.) Some of the wounds appeared to have been caused with a cutting instrument, and others had been done with a blunt instrument. From inquiries made I find that a small hatchet with a ham- mer on one side would be just such an instrument as would inflict the two kinds of wounds found on the de- ceased man's heat. Such a one was used for chopping firewood in the yard at the backof the shop in Victoria- street, occupied by the deceased. It was seen in the yard safe at five o'clock on Saturday evening, but was not there on Sunday morning, and has not been seen since. The younger prisoner made a statement on Sunday morn- ing, and since on several occatsione, that he and his father were stopped by two men and he got away and saw his father fall out of the trap. That statement about the two men cannot be borne out by any other evidence at all as far as we are able to ascertain. Some blood has been found upon the wearing apparel of both prisoners. I ask you to kindly remand them on this charge until Monday next. The Magistrates' Clerk (to Richard Davies).--Have you any questions to ask the Superintendent.? Richard Davies.—l beg pardon. The Magistrates' Clerk repeated the question, and Richard replied, No. Only I think he has made a little mistake about the time I got home. It was before eleven when I got home. Superintendent Leah.—l could not say exactly what the time was. That is only hearsay, as to what time he got home. In reply to a similar question George Davies replied, in a low voice, "No, Sir." Mr. Bellyse.—Then you will be remanded until Mon- day at one o'clock. Mr. Williams was present in the court on behalf of Mr. C. S. Brooke, of Nantwich who is prosecuting on behalf of the Crown. The prisoners were net legally represented. The elder prisoner, Richard Davies, is rktker stoutly built, with a slight dark moustache, dark. hair nearly black, and a round face with dark eyes': George the younger toy, is nearly seventeen years of affe. and is the same height as his braber, but of ' slighter build. He has a rather sullerkblook. His hair, like his brother's is very dark. The dress of both brothers appeared to be rather slovenly. The arrest has caused intense excitement in the neigh- bourhood and in Crewe where very few people heard of it until the evening. ANOTHER SENSATION. CONFESSION OF THE MURDER.

The startling developments in connection with the tragedy near Crewe reached their climax on Thursday night, when it was made known that the two sons of the murdered man, Richard Davies and George Davies, had confessed the part they had taken in connection with the commission of the crime. The police are very reti- cent, but what had all along been anticipated has turned out correct, that the youth who drove the trap made a false statement of what took place on the night of the murder, and that he did se to screen his brother. Both prisoners have made statements.inerimi- nating each other, from which it appears that the crime was planned by the murdered man's son Richard, and connived in by the younger prisoner. the circumstances are of a most painful character. The police have gath- ered sufficient evidence without requiring to call the younger prisoner as Queen's evidence. The most dread- ful part of the affair, however, is that th 4 mother will be required to give evidence against her sons, on the charge of wilfully murdering their father, and that sisters and brothers will also have to give evidence. The elder prisoner,. Richard Davies, who left on the night of the murder to walk home, wore an overcoat and gaiters. These have been found at his house, and are covered with blood splashes from top to bottom. The police are now searching for the missing axe, with which it is believed the murder was committed. POST-MORTE2If ON THE DECEASED.,-"'

Doctors Matthews, of Nantwich, and Vaughan, of Haslington' on Thursday, mad,e a post-rnortern examina- tion of the body of the murdered man avies. I FUNERAL OF THE vionm.—PAINFUL INCIDENTS AT THE GRAVESIDE. The funeral of the ' murdered man, Richard Davies, took place on Thursday afternoon, in the 'little village of Haslington, about six miles from The Hough. The funeral party were contained in three mourning coaches; and the body in a hearse. The coffin was covered with beautiful floral tributes sent by friends. The cortege left the Hough at two o'clock, and proceeded by road to Crewe, passing over the place on the high- way where the deceased was murdered. Little groups of villagers gathered at -places ou the route, and much sympathy was expressed with the widow and family. The widow was too prostrated by the terrible developments following the murder to leave her room, but the mourning coaches contained the eldest son of the deceased, John Davies, and three brothers—Fred, Tom, and Arthur—whose ages ranged from five to eight. The little fellows displayed much grief. An elder daughter, Emma Davies, was also present, and several friends. The cortege passed through Crewe to liaslingten. On arriving at the burial place. which is attached to the little Congregational chapel, a delay took place, through the grave not being of sufficient dimensions to receive the coffin. The gravediggers set I to work to widen it, and meanwhile the first portion of the service was conducted in the chapel by the Rev. A. W. Potts, Congregational minister, of Crewe. On going to the graveside it was found that the grave was still too small, and the minister and family and spectators stood by in the drizzling rain for a con- siderable time, while the gravediggers enlarged the sides of it. The delay was most painful. Eventually the coffin was brought to the graveside, but there was still some difficulty in lowering it to the bottom, on account of the narrow dimensions of thetrench. When, however, this had been done, the burial service was continued and completed. The weather during the long six miles journey was foggy and dark, with a drizzling rain; but notwithstanding this, a great number of persons were present in vehicles and on foot.

It is reported from New .York that a family of eight persons were, on Wednesday, poisoned by a negress servant at Point Pleasant, Virginia. Four of them have died, and the rest are in a precarious state. Mr. Frith, a wealthy resident Of Troy, U.S., has been shot dead by Mrs. Warneeker, a widow, with whom he had had improperrelations, who was enraged at discover- ing that Frith was married. The Vienna newspapers, on Thursday, reported a most serious riot among the glassworkers in the distriet of Gablonz, Bohemia, thecentre of the glass trade. Five hundred of the men attacked some of the glass-cutting rills, at Newdorf and Wiesenthaw, and broke up the machinery. There were several conflicts between the police and the rioters, of whom two were killed and ; several wounded. On Wednesday evening the military force stationed at Richenberg was despatched to the scene of the agitation. POLICE COURT.

On Monday morning, at -t-h-e-iiiarrington Borough Police Court, Alderman Davies, who presided, said that in the absence of the Mayor it was his duty to refer to the death of their late colleague Mr. Sleekly, who was one of the earliest magistrates connected with the com- mission issued for Warrington, and who was in a great measure the father magistrate of the bench, Through his discretion and wisdom he became chairman of the Court of Sessions in the Liverpool district. It we with respect that they spoke of his mernory.—Aldermau Harrison said that wherever the late Mr. Bleckly went he left behind him the impression that he-,was a matt of acute intellect, superior attainmentS, and sound judgment. They could not part with such a man without feeling that they had suffered a great loss. That lost extended far beyond the limits of Warrington. for during' his time Mr. 131eckly had performed great and valuable services,, which would be missed wherever, he was known.— Alderman Sutton, the other justic,e on the Bench, con- curred with th 4 remarks of his brother magistrates.

THE BOARD OF GUARDIANS. 'At the meeting of the Warrington Board f d Guardians, on Wednesday, the Chairman (Rev. G. F. Roberts, M.A.), after referring to the fact that he and Mr. Sutton, the clerk, attended the funeral of Mr. Bleckly said :—We thought it would be your desire that you should be repre- sented on the occasion. Moreover it was our individual wish to be present to show the greatest respect in our knowiag well, as both us had and excellence. Mr. Blackly has rpeasoowerir tathhei sd we poarrt ht e d, departed'thit life ripe in years, wisdorn, and eitpenence, and his loss would be appreciable in any neighbourhood. It distinctly creates •a void.' Warrington has especial cause for regret; for though he was not one of her sons, in the sense of being born there, still he spent his best years in that town and identified himself most usefully, during that time, with all, or most, matters of public in- terest, being twice elected mayor of the borough. He was closely connected with her industries and manufac- tures, being for some time president of her Chamber of Comulerce ; while the world-famed firm of Messrs. Pear- son, Knowles, and Co. continues, and we may hope will long continue, an abiding testimony to his capacity and organis:n'g powers. For many years he presided over the deliberations of this Board with the greuest advan- tage, gelding the members (as he always did) to sound i conclusions n the different matters that during that lengthened period called for their attention. He was a magistrate for both Lancashire and Cheshire,and perhaps his value in that capacity is besttestified by the faaof his election to succeed Lord Derby as Chairman of the Court of Quarter Sessions for the Hundred of West Derby, the duties of which honourable position he discharged with his usual ability, though it is to be feared in the result with too much anxious care. Not only was Mr. Bleckly thus a man of affairs, he was also a ripe scholar, a man of thought, sound judgment, and literary capacity. The Chairman moved that a vote of condolence with the family of the late Mr. Bleckly be passed. Alderman Harrison seconded the motion, and referred to the sterling ability Mr. Bleckly displayed in every- thing he took in hand, and to his usefulness in the various offices he filled. He was sure Warrington wculd be a long time beforeshe saw another /se. Henry Sleekly. The motion was passed. 'MAGISTERIAL REFERENCE AT NEWTON.

F. Gooch and T. D. Grimke." Colonel McCorquodale said that before commencing the business of the court it was his duty, as it had been on a great many oceasions. to allude to the death of a magistrate. He meant the death on the previous day of Mr. Sleekly. Jle remarke'd that he nbticedsOme of the papers had stited his age to be 67 years but he thought that must be, a mistake. He thought the late Mr. Sleekly must ha v't been 77 years of age. It was his (Colonel McCorquodale's) good fortune to sit along with him for 15 or 20 years at the Warring- ton Board of Guaraians, at the Warrington Sanitary Authority and at the Warrington Assebsrnent Committee, - and he also met him and acted with him on many occa- sions at Liverpool Sessions. They all knew that some years ago on the retirement of Mr. Gibbon the then deputy-chairman of the Quarter Sessions at Liverpool, Mr. Bleckly was appointed as his successor without any opposition and he was unanimously appointed to fill the vacant position. Last year on Lord Derby retiring from the chairmanship of the Quarter Sessions which he had held for a very long number of years Mr. Meekly was Un- animously chosen as the chairmen. He was a most able man, and a most useful man in his time and he would be a great loss to the magisterial bench at Liverpool and at l'reston. div.p: DEATH OF HENRY DE TOURVILLE.

The death is announced in the gaol at Barlan, Styria, of Henry de Tourville, whose trial for the murder of his wife, an English lady, by pushing her over a precipice on Mount Stelvio, in the Tyrol, caused a. great sensation ten years ago. De Tourville was tried in Austria, and, being found guilty of murdering his wife with the object of gaining possession of her property, was sen- tenced to imprisonment for life.

TEIC LABOUR MOVEMENT.

Mr. A. B. Forwood, M.P., speakin.. at Skelmersdale on. Saturday night, opposed any legislation with respect to the Eight Hours movement, and said the needs of each district could be met by combinations of workmen. STRIKE OF LONDON LABOURERS. There were 470 labourers on strike at Hay's Wharf, London, on Monday, consequent on a dispute about meal times. Tom Mann attendedat Haye's Wharf, and, addressing the men, exhorted them to remain out. He Was arrested at noon by the police. The Cumberland Coil Miners on Tuesday, accepted an advance of 10 per cent. They had asked for an advance of 15. LIVERPOOL DOCK LAD3IJRERS STRIKE. Matters were very quiet at the Liverpool doeics on ' Tuesday, and with a few exceptions work proceeded as usual. During the lnit few days large numbers of men have joined the Dock Labourers' 'Union' the membership of which is locally said 'to consist of about 7,500 men. The unsettled state of the dock labourers still continues to manifest itself in the warehouses and quays along the whole line of docks, and there is an evident disposition on the part of the men to do what they can towards helping those who are actually on strike.

_ Chemical THB chemical labourers of St Helens Labourers' and Widnes are organizing for the Union. protection of their own interests ; and, as they are a hard-worked and not over-paid body of men, it is to be hoped they will be success- ful in establishing their Union upon a sound and permanent basis. It is undeniable that they have just as much right to combine as their employers have; and yet sorne of the men have a fear that they will he victimised if they are known to take an active r art in the organisation. There was, on Sunday afternoon, a well-attended meeting, at St. Helens. of the branch which is being formed there; and it was intended to select the Yard Committees at this gathering, bat from representations which had been made as to the possibility of their being spies in the camp, it was deemed advisable to post- pone this part of thebusiness, leaving each yard to meet separately and elect its own committee. Mr. P. J. KING, who is acting as organiser, remarked that he thought they were strong enough to do everything in the light of day, and intimated that the men would be inclined to retaliate, if any of the Committee were treated with injustice. In view of the element of uncertainty and distrust, ii would be well if some of the leading employers would make it known that no workman need feai that he will jeopardise his position by trying tc help himself and his fellow labourers. The em- ployers can afford to do it, and it would put an end to what is, we trust, a needless alarm. A strong Union should be of service to the masters as well as the men, in that it will ensure something like uniformity in the trade, both as to hours and wages. One of the rules provides that—" No yard or works should give notice to enter into a strike until it has receivec the sanction of at least three-fourths of the yari committee, and until it is brought properly befole the branch committee, and thare must be at leaat three-fourths of the branch committee in favour of a strike before it was entered upon or continueL" It will be seen from this double check that tlare is no likelilgood of ill-considered strikes bebg

entered upon. As Mr. KING justly observed, "if the men were only patient, and they coald show the public they had a just and reasonable claim, and they were backed up by a strong and powerful Union, the masters would see the reasonableness. of their demands and strikes would be averted." No action has been taken as yet with the object of reducing the average working hours per week; but it may be presumed that that is a matter 'which will receive attention as soon as the Union feels itself strong enough to act. It will be re- membered that it was a St. Helens chemical worker who wrote, not long since, to Mr. G 1 STONE, and disclosed that he and many others were in the habit of working on an average 84hours Per week—that is 56 hours one week and 112 hours every other week. We have a strong opinion that this is a state of things which calls for a ' speedy remedy, and tril4 that when the employers are approached on the subject they will let it be seen that theY are desirous of overcoming whatever difficulties may at present block the way to reasonable hours of working. Opinion is now in favour of bringing the hours of labour below nine per daY; but is it not first necessary, we would ask, to deal with cases of really excessive hours? There is net at the present moment any large body of un- employed labour—speaking of the country 591 i whole—and what there is would probably be absorbed if steps were taken to put an end at onee and for ever to the practice of working 112 hears in a single week. It is satisfactory to °haat° that the new Union will be "registered accordie4 to law," which will be some sort of guarantee for the proper use of the funds. The members 110! only to be reasonable, courageous, and true wd each other, to ensure the suceess of a large all valuable organisation.

The Late Mr. HENRY BLECICLY, whose remaini has been sustained by the death of were interred at Bowdon Church, on Monday. lie was One of the ablest, if not the ablest, of tl°l magistrates for the County of Lancaster; and tli,Lsl was fittingly recognised when he was made Chauil man of the Liverpool Quarter Sessions. The had been previously held by Lord DERBY, fißait )0. a high tribute to the knowledge, experience, 04 judicial capacity of the late Mr. 13LECELY to 631-11 that there was never a doubt from the first that 'lel would prove a worthy successor. The " Liverpool Mercury " truly says :—" As a gentleman '4o° devoted his ripe years and experience gratuitoilall to the public service, he stands out conspicuous'l. as a typo of a class of whom Englishmen maY justly proud." When Lord DERBY retired fre°l- - the Kirkdale chairmanship, he suggested the advisability of appointing a professional chairrnaniu: and the question is again under consideration through the death of Mr. BLECKLY. The duties • increase as our laws increase, and it is felt that someone specially trained in the law should Pre' side over the magistrates. It is not to be f°l- - that there are magistrates and magistrate* and it is rare indeed for laymen to possess culture, experience, and above all the judicial hatO, of mind which were so strikingly characteristic °I , the late chairman. He had liveid a long life, ead;

he had spent his time wisely, or he could not, in addition to superintending a large business, have employed his pen so freely and so frequently in matters relating to literature and to commerce. But in this respect lie was another exemplification Of the savinc, that it is the busiest men who find most time to do things. Mr. BLECKLY was twice Mayor of Warrington; and had, too, been chair- man of such institutions as the Board of Guar- (aians, Chamber of Commerce, Literary and Philosophical Society, and the Conservative Asso- ciation. But his sphere in the later years of life was more than local; and his loss is to-day recognised as a loss to Lancashire.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

It is gratifying to see that so many towns and Local Board districts are adopting the Compulsory Act for the Notification of Infectious Diseases. Warrington, in this part of the country, led the way years ago. The members of the Haydock Local Board have taken a month to think the matter over but they will adopt the act if they are as Prudent as they are believed to be.

It is stated that Mr. Edison has received a cable from the German Government, expressing a desire to introduce immediately into the German public schools the Edison phonograph, and asking for an estimate for a large number of machines for that purpose. This is going ahead in the matter Of teehnical.education. Will John Bull ever show himself really alive on the subject?

No need to say—" Play up, Warrington l" so far aa the Gymnasium team are concerned. They did Play up on Saturday in the competition,in London, for the 200 Guinea Challenge Shield ; ang beat the Exeter Hall team by four points out of 274. saving scored in the first round, they have only to keep it up" to be hailed, finally, with the de- lightful strains of " See the conquering heroes Carrie !"

The Working Men's Committee in connection "with the Warrington Infirmary and Dispensary do their work exceedingly well; they have this Year raised £475, an increase upon last year of Over £45. They are fortunate in having such an !Idmirable Hon. Secretary as Mr. Z, Armitage, who 1,8 deserving of all the praise that was Oven him at Ihe annual meeting on Saturday. There is about to be an addition to the Infirmary, Provision being made for Medical Wards. Alder- Davies having regard to the services rendered 37 the lato Beamont suggested that, if, they bad a separate dispensary, it Shordd lie called "The -u'earnont Dispensary." It would, hOWeVel', 166 A • rather equivocal compliment to a good man's Inemory, coming as a second thought, after the failure of the " Beamont Memorial Fund." It I,l:lsight lead, too to confusion seeing that the word pensary is already a part of the title of the Whole institution.

, Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., colliery proprie- '°/'s, are to be commended for bringing two of their servants before the magistrates for breach of he Mines Regulation Act. It was their duty to inspect the Boston mine, at Haydock, within a aPecified time, with a view to ensuring the safety the miners, and this they had failed to do. As the ease was not pressed, the offenders were fined '4. and costs each only. But this should be a Warning to them. An accident which should result !Ion) such sheer disregard of the law would be in the nature of a crime.

Parliament opens, on the 11th February. Mr. Smith, in his circular to his followers in the House, of Commons, refers to " questions of great import- ance" being" at once submitted." Lord Salisbury addressing the Peers, merely says "it is probable that important business will be submitted.' Why should it be " probable" only ? If the lords are worth their salt, why cannot they set about ar- ranging that of a " certainty" they will do some- thing important? Would their lordships have it understood that, as ornamental people, they play at politics—except when there is mischief to do ? Well, as things go, we shall have to either end them or mend them, some day.

It will be seen from the report (given in another column) that the sub-Committee appointed by the General Purposes Committee of the Warrington Town Council have gone very carefully into the question of the duties and emoluments attaching to the Town Clerkship. On the face of it, it would seem that Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, as the new Town Clerk, will cost more to the town with a salary of £5OO a year, and with a clerk, office, and office boy in addition; but we understand that these " extras " will be more than met by the " extras " in the shape of fees which he will save or surrender. More than this, it is determined that he shall have no private practice. The recommendation of Mr. Whittle's appointment will be considered, and, we believe, sanctioned at the meeting of the Council on Tuesday next.

-- The "Land of Nod" was the appropriate title of an interesting lecture on Dreams, given by the Rev. Gibson Smith, on Saturday, before the mem- bers of the St. Paul's Mutual Improvement Society. He contended that "every person when asleep dreamt, although they did not always remember it." Are we to surrender, then, the "dreamless sleep' of childhood as a pretty fiction? Surely there is such a thing as sound—that is dreamless sleep. The scriptures tell us that " A dream cometh through the multitude of business" ; but there are business men now-a-days who are similiar- ly disturbed when there is no business to be done. It is a good thing to secure easy digestion and an easy mind, for —to quote Shakespeare, who wrote wisely of dreams as of everything else—" Un- strained thoughts do seldom dream on evil."

div.head: DISHONEST DOMESTIC SERVANT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A DISHONEST DOMESTIC SERVANT AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Catherine Smith (18), whose parents reside at Widnes, wascharged with having stolen ss. belonging to Thomas Heath Bar- ton, of the George Inn, Pool-lane. The prisonei who had beon a domestic servant at the Inn since the Bth January, was suspected of theft, and on Sunday Mr. Barton searched her box and found ss. wrapped in paper there. As she had borrowed 3d. from him on the previous Sunday to pay her fare across the Bridge, he gave her into the custody of P.C. Crowder, to whom she admitted that she had stolen the money. The prisoner said she had been brought up honestly and made a most pathetic appeal for mercy, and the Bench acting on the prosecutor's wish for a lenient sentence, imposed a fine of 10s. including Costs. ALLEGED TREFT OF GOLD RINGS AT RUNCORN. Eliza Anderson, a "stranger," was brought before the Runcorn bench of magistrates to answer a charge of stealing two gold wedding rings, value two guineas the property of William Marsh, pawnbroker, Church-st. About nine o'clock, on Saturday night, the prisoner entered the shop and said she wanted a wedding ring, at the same time stating she was sanity; for America on Wednesday. A case of linos were shown her, and Mr. Marsh saw her secure two between her finger and thumb and go on examining the remainder. He then placed the rings in their positimns in the box and walking round the counter found that the woman had concealed one in her breast. He gave her into the custody of P.S. Gosling, and afterwards a second ring was discovered lying on the floor near where the prisoner had been stand- ing. The prisoner was remanded for a week in order that inquiries might be made into her antecedents. AN HAM Way TO HELP THE Poo.—For every half-pound of Collier's Is. Tea purchased by persons who attend St. Michael's or Old Parish Church, Walter Collier will give one mows of this splendid Tea (neatly wrapped) to the District Nurse for distribution among her patients. Directions: The tinfoil wrappers to be sent to 6, Church-st., with name and address of sender written oa the inside.—Arlet.

A STRANGE HIDING PLACE FOR Goo AT RUNCORN, Before Mr. H. Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas, at Run- corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Louisa Spencer, a young woman of bad character, was charged with having on the 23rd January stolen £l5, belonging to Louisa Chesters, her mother, an old woman who resides in Canal-st. It was alleged that on Saturday, the 20th January, Mrs. Chesters had £lOl in a bag which was sewn in her stays, the whole of the sum being in gold. On Wednesday she susre,-,ted that her stays had been tampered with and on counting the money found there was only £B6 in the bag. The woman accounted for being in possession of this large sum by stating that last summer she drew £2OO out of the Sandbach Savings Bank, and had placed a portion in the Post Office Savings Bank. She informed the Bench that she charged her daughter with having taken the money and that the latter replied. " I will give you your money back."--Superintendent Large said the police had made inquiries and had ascertained that the prisoner had really spent no money during the past week. The woman had told several different stories about the money, and he thought she did not really know what money she had. Some time ago she charged her husband with having stolen some money which she had missed.—The prisoner denied the theft, and the magistrates considering the evidence unsatisfactory dis- charged her.—Mr. Reynolds advised the woman to place her money in the Bank at once, and she promised to do so.

D. Herring; air, "Arm, arm, ye brave," Mr. Frank Whitworth; song, "Spring time," Miss Clara Taylor; recitation, Miss Tyrie ; song, ‘• Che Faro," Miss Pierpoint ; flute solo, "Le Reve," Mr. W. Ockleston ; song, "It was a dream," Miss Jessie Pritchard ; violin solo, "Hungarian Dances," Mr. El. D. Herring. Interval. Pianoforte duet, "Faust," Miss Edith Crosby and Mr. Wynne Humphreys; song. "The devout lover," Mr. Frank Whitworth; flute solo, "The blind girl to her harp," Mr. W. Ockleston ; song, "The Toilers," Niss Pierpoint ; violin solo caprice, Mr. H. D. Herring; sung, "Joyous Life," Miss Jessie Pritchard; song, "The Skipper," Mr. Frank Whitworth; galop, " Qui vive,' Miss Edith Closby and Mr. Wynne Humphreys. All who took part in the performance, including dose who came from a distance, are well- known in Runcorn and their efforts were fully appreci- ated by the members of the class and their friends who had assembM in considerable force. Encores were numerous aud altogether a pleasant evening was spent. Mr. Humphreys was the conductor.

MORE COAL STEALING AT WIDNES.

James Shaw, of Old Marsh,Widnes, was brought beforp the magistrates, on Monday, charged with stealing 56 lbs. of coal belonging to the London and .North-Western Rail- way Company. About 3 o'clock on Sunday afternoon P.C. Worsfold and Detective AtkinsQn saw the prisoner get upon a wagon at the Old Marsh, and throw a lump of coal to the ground. He then got down and was walk- ing away with the coal on his head when he was appre- hended. Ile was sentenced to a month's hard labour. RUNCORN' TONIC Son FA CHOIR CONCERT.

For the second time this season, the sol-farists of Run- corn will challenge public criticism on Monday evening when they give a grand concert in Runcorn Public Hall. Under the guidance of Mr. J. div.head: BRUTAL WIFE BEATER AT WIDNES.
div.p: A BRUTAL WIFE BEATER AT WIDNES.

On Tuesday, at Widnes Police Court, Wm. Gray, a chemical labourer, at the British Alkali works, was brought. up on remand charged with unlawfully wound- ing his wife Mary. The parties live at 27 IVlidwood-st., and on the 20th January the prisoner went home drunk at noon. His dinner was not ready and he commenced to abuse his wife, concluding by throwing a paraffin lamp at her. The missile struck her on the forehead and knocked her senseless to the ground. While she lay there the prisoner kicked her in a most ferocious fashion and the poor woman, according to Dr. Hutchinson's testi- mony was very severely injured. The prisoner was corn- mitte.d to take his trial at the County Quarter Sessions.

div.head: BISHOP OF CHESTER AT RUNCORN._
div.p: THE BISHOP OF CHESTER AT RUNCORN._

On Thursday night, a special service was held in Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, in aid of the Improvement Fund. There was a good congregation. The Bishop of Chester was present, and preached a good sermon from the words "Be ready always to give an answer to every man that asked' you a reason of the hope that is in you, with meekness and fear." His Lordship proceeded to give an outlina, reasons for, with faith in the church, and in conclusion he asked them to think this matter out, and to be earnest, thoroughgoing, solfdenying, studying, labouring churchmen. The prayers were read by the Rev. Dr. Preston, and the lessons by the Rev. Canon Greenall (who officiated as the Bishop's Chaplain) and the Rev, W. Sanderson (Curate). 13ngn v. CiDER.

A Man named Johr-i-0;;;;(;iiii;as---brought up at Run- corn Police Court, on Thursday, charged with having been drunk and disorderly in the Half Way House, Halton-road, and also with assaulting P.C. On the previous evening the prisoner entered the house and was supplied with a glass of beer by Gregory, the land- lord, who afterwards discovered that the man was drunk, and refused to supply his further wants except in the way of cider. The prisoner told him to take his cider to--, and created a disturbance. P.C. div.head: ROURVAIRS BY NAVVIRS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ROURVAIRS BY NAVVIRS AT RUNCORN.

Two navvies, named Henry Jackson and Henry Wood- field, were brought up at Runcorn Police Court, on Thurs- day, charged with stealing a coat from the shop of Messrs Craddock and Son, pa.witbrokers, Church-street; and a coat from the shop of Arnold linsworth, High-street. The prisoners were further charged with stealing a bottle, containing a pint and a half of whisky, from the Devonshire Hotel, Ashridge-street, the property of Mr. J. W. Lightburn. One of the prisoners was seen to take a coat from a hook outside Craddock's shop and, information being given to P.C. Worth, he traced and apprehended the prisoners, upon whom the other articles were also found. In order that inquiries might be made into their antecedents, the prisoners were remanded for a week. BREAKING A POLICEMAN'S FINGER AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court on Tuesday, John Higgins of Dock-st., was charged with being drunk and disorderly and further with causing grievous bodily harm to P.C. Simpson. About midnight on Monday the prisoner, who was drunk, was creating a disturbance near St. Ambrose Church, Halton View. As he would not give his name and address, P.C. Simpson took him /alto custody, when the prisoner became very violent, and in the struggle ' both men fell to the ground. Simpson attempted to put the handcuffs on his prisoner while on the ground, but the prisoner seized the third finger on the constable's right hand, and twisted it in such a manner as to break it. The officer however stuck to his man and eventually , got him to the police station. The prisoner was re- manded until Monday. , UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN,

It will be remembered that there were eight candidates, who presented themselves, and it is satisfac- tory to know that no fewer than seven have succeeded in satisfying the Examiner, while two have passed with distinction. The result is appended—passed with dis- tinction (in order of merit) first, (with prize), Emily J. Clayden ; 2nd, H. Head. The following satisfied the Examiner (in alphabetical order) : Mary E. Benbow, Charles Ditchfield, Mary Elizabeth Naylor' John Shingler ' and Alice Mary Taylor. The second lecture of the course on Physiography, under the University Extension Scheme, was delivered by Mr. Mac Kinder, on Tuesday evening, to a large audience. The subject "Volcanoes," VViLS dealt with in a hig'.ly interesting and Intelligible , form, and applause was frequent. Mr. H. W. Handley manipulated the oxy-hydrogen lantern by which the lecture was illustrated. There are now 50 members of the Students' Association. LECTURE ON. RITUALISM AT RUNCORN.

In the --G-OS'pel Mission-room, Duke's Field, a few evenings ago, Mr. Robert Foulkes, of Frodsham, gave a brief description of Ritualism. Commencing his argu- ment from Scripture, the Apostle's Creed, Litany, Homilies, he contrasted the teaching of such men as Littledale, Pusey, Grace and other of the Romanizing fraternity inside the Church of England, making special reference to the Society of the Confraternity of the Blessed Sacrament, showing that they teach the real presence, and that every bit of bread or wafer and wine till consumed contain Christ in his entirety. Similar teaching was found in the life of Bishop King. They advocated prayers for the dead in direct opposition to to their ordination vows—" To be ready at all times to banish and drive away all false doctrine and erroneous teaching." The Bible distinctly in the following places condemn-id this Road sh teaching: —Eccles. 9c.. Psa.lls c., Job 14 c., Isa. 38c., 63c. He alluded to Mass being recently said for the late Rev. Ma,ckonockie, and to the practice of placing a cross over the grave in order to secure the faithful repose of the departed. He referred to the teaching that the chancel of the Church was the Holy of Holies and that the laity were to be driven in the nave as their proper place, the chancel only being for these would-be priests wha are not found in Ephesians 4c.11 v. In conclusion, Mr. Foulkes brought evidence to prove that Ritualism was Romanism.—A workingman asked, bow it was that the Bishop did not put down this Ritualism ? If the clergy are under state control, why are they not treated as the officers in the army awl navy, and made to do their duty. If they will not do so disestab- lish the Church and let them go any way they please. A vote of thanks was given to the Lecturer, and a wish expressed to hear him again. PROPOSED MEMORIAL TO THE LITE MR. IMISON OF
WIDNES.

For the purpose of considering the question of the erection of a memorial to the late Mr. J. B. Imison, meeting of the parishioners of Widnes, was held in the National School, on Monday evening. There was a fair attendance. Mr. H Wade Deacon who presided, said as to the desirability of having a memorial they were all agreed, and the main point to consider was, what form the memorial should take.—The Vicar (Rev. G. H. Garrett), said the Church Council considered it better that the parishioners themselves should decide. Three schemes were mentioned : one was that an organ should be erected in St. Paul's Church, the second was that the memorial should take the form of a stained glass window and the third was that a wing or room of the new parochial building should be called the unison Memorial Room, and coupled with this that there should be a tablet erected, dedicating the room to his memory. —Mr. F. Neil moved that a wing of the new parochia' room be called the unison Memorial Room and that a stained glass window be erected to his memiary in St. Paul's Church.—Mr. John Hough seconded the proposi- tion and he remarked that he was with Mr. unison on the last Sunday that he attended .church, when the whole of their conversation centred upon the new parochial room, in which he took such a deep interest, and he thought they ought to do all they could to see that it was completed, and thus carry out the wishes of him whose removal by death they all so deeply deplored.—Mr. J. C. Crawford supported the proposal, which was carried, and it was further resolved that the bulk of the money subscribed should be devoted to the wing of the parochial room and the balance spent in erecting a stained glass window in St. Paul's Church.— The Church Council were requested to carry out the scheme and that a committee be formed on which St. Paul's Choir should be represented.—A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the proceedings.

ALLEGED ROBBERY FROM THE SHIP CANAL CONTRACTOR
AT R UNCORII.

Before Major Elaziehurst and Mr. G. L. Wigg at Run- corn Police Court, on Thursday. Peter Connell, alias Polisher, and Andrew Connell, his son, were charged with stealing 4 cwt. of coal the property of the executors of the late Mr. T. A. Walker, contractor to the Ship Canal Company. Mr. Shelley, walking ganger, said the contractor had a quantity of coal stored in Speakman's yard and about eight o'clock that morning, he saw the prisoners taking coal from a boat and place it into bags. He went to the yard, and saw that the coal had dis- appeared from lhere. Afterwards be found a bag of co/4 at the Ferry slip. The coal was similar to that of the prosecutors. The prisoners were apprehended, and stated that the coal had been in the boat all night. They denied the theft.—The Bench considered the evidence insufficient, and discharged the prisoners.

div.head: CO-OPERATIVE SOIREE AND BALI, AT RUNCORN,
div.p: CO-OPERATIVE SOIREE AND BALI, AT RUNCORN,

_ The annual soiree aud ball in connection with the Runcorn Co-operative Society was held in the Public Hall on Wednesday evening. Between 700 and 800 persons were present at the tea party with which the proceedings commenced, and, fortunately, the Committee had made ample provision for so large a number and there was no lack of substantial fare. Afterwards the room was cleared, and a concert was held under the presidency of Mr. Royle who made an appropriatespeech. The Secretary gave some figures which showed that the Society was in a most flourishing condition. Mr. W. H. Norman, comic vocalist, was the chief entertainer and the audience much enjoyed his character sketches. Mr. J. Woods, gave a cornet solo in his usual skilful manner. From ten o'clock until the early hours of the morning a ball was held, but the room was too crowded for a proper terpsichorean disf-y. LORD SALISBURY AND Si, HELENS CONSERVATIVES. In acknowledging the receipt of resolutions or confidence in the Government passed at recent Conservative meetings in St. Helens Lord Salis- bury's secretary writes :—" Lord Salisbury 4sires me to acknowledge with thanks the receipt of your letter of the 24th Chclosing A copy of the reso- lution passed 011 the 20th inst., by the constituents of Mr. H. Seton-Xarr. He has derived great satis- faCiden from the kind assurance of confidence and support which are teadered to him in the resolution by the members present at that meeting."

div.head: MESSRS. A. B. WALKEn .iNi3 SONS.
div.p: MESSRS. A. B. WALKEn .iNi3 SONS.

Arrangements are in progress, and will be com- pleted in a week or two. for the conversion of the business of Messrs. A. 13. Walker and Sons (Sir A. B. Walker, Bart.), into a limited liability company. It is understood the capital will be three or three and a half millions. The concern.is.not being " financed ' by any London house, and it is intended to secure to this district an equitable allotment of the share and debenture stock. It is stated that the profits of this great brewing firm last year amounted to a sum of nearly a quarter of a million. RAILWAY BREAKDOWN NEAR NEWTON...

An unpleasant incident occurred on the Railway near Newton-le-Willows, on Monday morning. When the 8.15 train from Wigan to Liverpool arrived at Lowton Junction it Iva,' found that the engine had broken down and could not proceed. The pas- sengers jumped out and ran to the ganchester and Liverpool line, where a Manchester train was stopped and conveyed the passengers to Newton-le-Willows, where they got the first available titan for their re- spective destinations. Meanwhile the Wigan train blocked the line at LoWton until a fresh engine was procured.

div.head: WARGRAVB SCHOOLS.
div.p: WARGRAVB SCHOOLS.

On Thursday evening a meeting was held in War- grave Schools, under the auspices of the 1..gm1 branch of the Church of England Temperance Society. The chair was occupied by the Rev Canon Whitley, rector, and there was a very large attendance not- withstanding the inclement weather. An excellent programme of musical selections was rendered by the school choir under the able leadership of Mr. James Davies, and a recitation, pianoforte duet, and action songs were also given. The entire per- formance reflected considerable credit upon those who had trained the juvenile artistes. The accom- panist was Miss Davies.

div.head: LANCABITIRE CouNTV COUNCIL.
div.p: LANCABITIRE CouNTV COUNCIL.

The Sea Fisheries Committee of the Lancashire County Council in their report, issued on Thursday morning,state that th eyh aye colleeted much valuable information, and that great interest is taken in the matter by fishermen and others. They recommend that application be made by the County Council to the Board of Trade for the creation forthwith of a Lancashire Sea Fisheries District, extending from Haverigg Point,-Cumberland, and from Hilbre Point, Cheshire past ililbre Island, seawards through the Fairway Bell Beacon. The agenda for the meeting of the County Council next Thursday comprises notices of motion that the Executive Cattle Plague Committee take steps to enforce the dtie licensing of dogs throughout the county, and to obtain returns from the police of the numberof doge in the county; that the duties likely to be assigned to a medical officer of health do not justify his appointment at a salary of £BOO a yelp.. FILTEIO.—J. 8. Garland, ironmonger, Bridge-street, War- rington.—Advt. Sr. IiBLENS IN DARKNESS.

The inhabitants ofSt. Helens hada7-singular ex- perience on Friday night, last week. Shortly before eight o'clock all the gas lamps, public and private were suddenly Pxtinguished. Many people rushed into the streets terrified, and a general commotion was occasioned when it was found that the streets were plunged in darkness. In the principal thorough- fares, the tradespeople were considerably alarmed for the safety of their wares, and during the exist- ence of the unexpected darkness there was a great rush on shops where candles and lamps were sold. A great deal of inconvenience was caused at Afse railway station, and at various places of meeting, but, happily, there was no- accident. The mains were supplied with gas in the course of about ten minutes. It appears that the mishap arose in the changing of the town's supply from one of the large gas-holders to a second holder, at the Corporation Gas Works in Warrington Old-road. The supply from the second holder was not turned on soon enough, and the gas in the first holder was exhausted about five minutes before the :second connection was complete.

div.head: SHOCKING SUDDEN DEATH OF A WORKMAN.
div.p: SHOCKING SUDDEN DEATH OF A WORKMAN.

A painful incident occurred at the Works of Messrs. T. and T. Vicars, engineers, Earlestown, on Saturday morning, when John Flannagan, 31 years of age, a moulder, living at 27 Grafton-et., was found lying in an unconscious condition, and death ensued Immediately afterwards. The deceased had enjoyed good health up to last week when he com- plained of a pain in his chest, which be thought arose from indigestion. He stayed from his work on the Monday and Tuesday, but did not call in any doctor. He went to his work from Wednesday until, Saturday morning; when, on returning tq his breakfast he said to his wife that he bad got the pain very bad that morning. He returned to the works about half-past eight, and on the way ;rimed several of his fellow workmen to wholn he spoke but he did not complain of any illness. A few minutes after he bad entered the works he was found lying unconscious 'in one of the fire-holes which be would have to pass on his way to the moulding shop: He was carried into the fitting shop, but he expired on the way. Dr. Valentine was immediately summoned and that gentleman attended, but, of course, his services were of no avail. The body was removed to deceased's late home. On Monday night Mr. S. Brighouse, County Coroner, held an inquest at the New Market Inn, Market-st., Earlestown. Evidence to the foregoing effect was given by Annie Flannigan, wife of deceased, John Lynch. a moulder, Robert Macklin, labourer, and Dr. Valentine, who attributed death to syncope brought on by an affection of the heart or through concus- sion of the brain caused by falling into the firehole. The jury returned a verdict of "Death from Natural Causes." PgTROLEITNE OIL.—J. S. Garland. 51, Brldge-straiff War- rlngton.—.eldvt.

div.head: HER 179TH APPHARANCIC.
div.p: HER 179TH APPHARANCIC.

The number of con ;lotions of Bridget Kildare, a notorious St. Helens character, are rapidly mount- ing. Sheagain appeared in the dock at the Town Hall, on Monday, and she was finmd 10s. and costs for being drunk and incapable in Tontine-street. This made her 179th conviction.

RAILWAY FATALITY AT GAILSWOOD. . On Th ursday morning, a shocking railway fatality occurred at Garswood, near St. Helens. It seems that a man named Stephens, who is employed as a ganger in the employ of Mr. Braddock,who is making certain railway extensions at Garswood, was follow- inn- his employment when he was knocked down and killed by a passenger train.

CONSERVATISM IS NORTH WIC II D [VISION. The annual general meeting of the North wick Division Conservative Registration Association was held at the Constitutional Club, Northwich. on Saturday. Mr. Joseph Verdin presided. Mr. C. J. Hughes. the secretary, read the annual report, in which he stated that 361 new claims and 82 objec- tions were sustained. , The question of a Comerea- Live candidate for the division had engaged the earnest attention of the committee, who hoped soon to secure a candidate who would have the united and energetic support of all sections of the Unionist part Y. The financial statement showed a deficit of £142 Bs., which was re4uced by £lO. received since the accounts were made 'up.--The reports were adopted.—The Chairman announced his resignation of the presidency of the Association, stating that it would be to the benefit of all concerned if the diffe- rent parts of the constituency were better repre- sented. He should continue to promote the welfare of the Conservative cause in the future ache had in the past. (Applause.) On the proposition of Mr. .1. W. Lightburn (Runcorn), seconded by Mr. Newell, Colonel France-Ha.yhtirst, of Bostoek Hall, was elected president. A large number of vice presidents were also appointed. Those for Runcorn district were: Messrs. John Brundrit, S. B. Chadwick, William Hayes, F. A. Lake, Joha Ockle- stone, WalterrWigg,, Henry Reynolds, C. W. Hazlehurst, :G. L. Wigg, W. Whittaker, Revs. W. Preston and A. Maitland Wood, and Dr. Steele. Mr. T. Ward was re- elected Chairman of the Association. Mr. Newell was ! appointed hon.sec. and Mr. C. F. Parr, treasurer. It , was proposed that Messrs. J. Vertiin, W. H. Verdin and! J. Newell be the representatives elf the association on the Council of the Lancashire and Cheshire Union of Con- servative Associations.—Mr. W. H. Verdin pointed oat that he now lived in the Eddisbury Division, and stated that they ought to have some one qualified by residence. for their representative. Now he was on his feet, he should like to say a word in explanation of the reason why his subscription to the,association had not been as large as previously. In 1888 he reduced his subscription from £5O to £10; and in 1889 he further reduced it to £5. Without wishing to appear boastful in any way, he might say that he could not plead poverty as the reason; but he did it as a kind of silent protest against certain things to which he took exception. (flea,r, hear.) He did not think it would be wise, nor yet to the interest of the Conservative party, to give any further explanation than to say that he felt it due to himself that he should enter some kind of protest against what had come to his ears. Eventually after soine discussion the three gentle- men named were elected.

div.head: tLOPEACIT AND RAILWAY ROBBERY AT HELSBY. .
div.p: tLOPEACIT AND RAILWAY ROBBERY AT HELSBY. .

---- William Allen, navvy on the Manchester Ship Canal, was charged, on remand, with stealing a lamp, value 7s. 61, on the 25th November, 1888, the pro- perty of the London and North-Western and Great Western Joint Railways, from Helsby Station. Mr. It. Preston, solicitor, prosecuted, and Mr. Pletcher defended. The evidence showed that the lamp was placed on a shelf in the porter's room, at Helsby Station, on the date in question, and was missed the following morning. Nothing was heard of it till the Bth inst., when a struggle took place at Helsbv Railway Station between Allen and his wife, the husband trying to take her watch and chain from her. She screamed and P.C. Turner went to the scene. She then told the officer that her husband had stolen a lamp from the station, and that he would find it in the pantry. Defendant replied that it was false, and further re- marked that if there was anything at his house belonging to the Railway Company, they were welcome to it. The Seigeant went to the house, and found the lamp as des- cribed, and thereupon Allen said he had purchased it from a man of whose present • whereabouts he was ignorant. The witnesses, in reply to Mr. Fletcher, said that when the struggle took place the defendant's wife was just about to elope with another man. P.S. Turner said Allen had conducted hi mself properly, and was con- sidered to be a very respectable trian.—Mr. Fietcher for the defence, urged that his client had hitherto been trusted with property, and had w,ver te,.tra.yel that trust. One morning he met a man known as " Sca,nn," who came to him and SA iti he was g Ang on tramp. lie had a lamp in his possession, and having no money, defendant gave him is. for it. Ile took the-ze valuables ft len he. , :bid the re o pm. out of rever-440, sly? the statement referred tc by P.S. Tit:nen—Fined 10s. and costs.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. H. Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas. DRUNKENNESS.—Martha Alice Crank and Sydney Arthur were each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness. STONE THRONVING.—John Royle and William Cooke, pleaded guilty to throwing stones in Ashridge-st., and were each fined ss. and costs. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—George Duckett, Church-et., was fined 6d. and costs Bs. 6d. for this offence. AN UNMUZZLED DOC4.—John Morris, grocer, was fined 64. and costs Bs. 64. for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled. PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday afternoon, when there were present Mr. J. W. Wareing, (deputy chairman) in the chair, Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Messrs. J. Birchall, J. Burchall, W. B. Longton, E. Syder, G. Davies, J. Leatherbarrow, J. Peover, W. A. Graves, J. Marsh, J. Kenwright, J. Ranson, J. Mercer, W. Middlehurst, W. Lowe, C. B. Johnson, W. Tyrer, W. Daine, J. Buckley, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). THE ClisinuaH.—Mr. Wareing intimated that the Chairman (the Rev. Dean Finegan) had requested him to .express his inability to attend the Board meeting in con- sequence of an engagement with his Bishop to visit some portion of the deanery. RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reperted that there were 60 inmates this week, 607 last week, 812 in the corresponding week last year; 43 vagrants had been relieved, against 56 in the same period last year. THE GUARDIANS AND THEIR DUTIES.—MT. Middlehurst drew attention to the fact that at one of the meetings of the Visiting Committee he was the only member who attended to inspect the workhouse. He thought something wanted doing to secure a better attendance of the Guardians at those meetings. There was never more sickness in the house than at present, and there were seven fatal cases in five days last week. There was so much sickness that a good number of the inmates who were washing and do- ing other work last week were now bedfast. It was important that there should bea quorum at the me-tings. —The Deputy Chairman said he was glad Mr. Middlehurst had raised that question, and he thought the Guardians on the rota for the Visiting Committee meetings should attend regularly or get some other Guardian to attend in their places.—Mr. Leatherbarrow said that was a grievance which had existed for 15 years past.—Mr. Tyrer : You might as well extend it to 20 years.—The subject then dropped. THE NORTHWICEI GUARDIANS AND PRESCOT WORKHOUSE. —A communication was read from the Clerk to the Northwich Union enclosing the following cope of a reso- lution which had been passed at a meeting of the Guar- dians of that Union on the 24th inst 6' Resolved that the thanks of the Guardians be given to the officers of the Prescot Union for the courteous way in which they received the Committee of this Board and afforde i them valuable information in reference to the buildings and arrangements of their admirable workhouse." THE AUDIT.—The Clerk nsad a report from the Govern- ment Auditor intimating that everything with respect to the Union finances were perfectly satisfactory; and he (the Clerk) added that be was happy to say that they had not any surcharges to meet. PAUPER LUNATICS.—The Clerk submitted a list of all lunatics, idiots and 'other persons of unsound mind chargeable to the Union, and giving other details.—Mr. Middlehurst remarked that he found the number of lunatics was still increasing, the present number being 20 over the previous year.—Mr. Daine asked if it was 6.10 t cus- tomary to have an annual inspection of asylums where Union lunatics were confined.—The Clerk replied that there was no stated periods for inspection.—Mr. Nine moved that a visit be paid to Rainhill asylum by the Guardians on Thursday next.—Mr. Marsh seconded and after some conversation the motion was adopted. Tina CHILDREN IN KIRKDALE ScHocas.—The Rev. S. A. K. Silveater drew attention to what he considered a necessity for more regular visits to Rirkdale Schools for the inspection of the Prescot Union children and ultimately moved "'that a Committee be formed con- sisting of the Very Rev. Dean Finegan, Rev. C. W. Wooll, Messrs. Wareing, W. B. Longton, Leatherbarrow, Marsh, Whalley, and the Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, with power to add to their number, from time to time as they,. shall think expedient to visit childreqof PreScot Union who are being educated at the KirkdalfiSchools and that they be asked to report to the Board after each such visit." After some discussion Mr. Graves seconded, and the

was•motion carried. Two or three Guardians asked if it would debar other Guardians from attending or visit- ng Kirkdale Schools and it was stated that the resolution would not have that effect. This was the principal business.
