div.head: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB. ANNUAL MEETING.
div.p: RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB. ANNUAL MEETING.

The first annual meeting of the members of this Club was helt). in the Committee-room, on Monday evening. Me W. Ockleston, the 'chairman, pre- sided. He said he was glad to say that the clue had so far done very well and had given general satisfaction. (Hear, hear.) They were not out of debt; they wanted money and they wanted more members so that the club might become of more use in the political world.—The Secretary, Mr. R. Moore, read the financial statement and remarked that the club was in a fairly good financial position, and if they could get a few more members they would be alr right. In answer to inquiries, the Secretary said there was about £36 owing on furnishing account, and there were sub- scriptions aue amounting to nearly £6O. The statement was adopted. The Secretary then presented a report which stated that although the club had only been in existence three months, there was every reason to be satisfied with the work done since the club was opened by Mr. Brunner, on October seventh. There were on the books 174 members and a further 24 were proposed for membership, making a total of 198. After referring to several other matters the secretary said he could not conclude his report without alluding to the death of Mr. Richard Wells who was a good Liberal and a hard worker in the cause and his loss would be felt very much. (Hear, hear.) The report was adopted unanim- ously.—On the proposition of Mr. J. Clark seconded by Mr. T. Clegg, it was resolved that the trustees shall be ex-fficio members of the General Committee. A diseussion took place on card playing, and eventually consideration of the subject was adjourned for a fort- night, in order that each member might be notified on the question.—The same course was taken as to a motion on the salary of the Secretary. Mr. J. T. Brunner. M.P., was unanimously elected president, and Mr. W. Ockles- ton, was appointed treasurer. There were 52 nomina- tion for 13 members of the Committee. The voting was by ballat, and resulted in the Committee being con- stituted as follows :—Messrs. A. R. Norman, J. Clarke, W. Handley. T. Clegg, F. Whalley, E. Marshall, B. Kniveton, T. Poole, T. Dean, R. Pierpoint, H. Wright, E. W. Humphreys, and John Bate.—A vote of thanks to the Chairthan, and to the various officials of the club concluded the proceedings.

Tlia Inspector r4e.po;:ted-ibat.fiCiiiciConferred with the rerresentatives of the townships of Weston and Clifton, respecting the suggested extension of the main sewer, at the higher end of Heath. road, in Weston village, for the interception of the sewage &c., from property be- longing to Mr. Joseph Pritchard of Runcorn and others. The sewage emanated from 12 houses and at present flowed upon an area of land about 130 yards in length and about4l yards in width and the conclusion arrived at was that if such land was properly managed, no ex- tension of sewer would be required and no nuisance would arise therefrom. It was decided that the question of extension remain in abeyance for the present.—The report was adopted.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. THE SURVEYOR ASKED TO RESIGN.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. THE SURVEYOR ASKED TO RESIGN.

A special meeting of this Board was held on Tues- ' day afternoon, at the offices at Widnes, for the purpose of further considering the action of the Surveyor (Mr. Higgineson) in regard to the Moss tank Sewerage Works. At the last ordinary meet- ing of the Board various allegations were made against. the Surveyor, the principal complaint against him being that he had allowed " extras " to a great amount to be incurred by the Board i i n respect to the sewerage works n question, and that the Highway Committee were unable to obtain from him any sufficient explanation in regard to them. The consequence was that the Highway Committee of the Board recom- mended that the Surveyor be asked to resign, but, after a good deal of discussion, in which the general! duties of the Surveyor were referred to, the recom- ' mendation was not passed, a decision being come to to the effect that a special meeting be held, at which the Surveyor would have the opportunity of replying to the charges that had been preferred against him. 'the chair was occunied ny Mr. F. H. Gossage, and there were also present Messrs. O'Keeffe, Sadler, H. Gaskell, jun., J. Houghton, J. Taylor, F. Heves, F. C. Liddell, it. Cook, J. Midweod, D. Wright; T. fiandley, J. Carey, J. T. Allen (clerk), and Higginson (surveyor). The Chairman, in introducing the subject of the meet- ing, said that it was the duty of the Board, as repre- senting the ratepayers, to go most closely into the matter that they were called upon to concich!r. Ile thought that the charge of "incompetency" sholild be with irawe, and that in its place the word " inefficiency "should be subst i tilted , The Clerk (Mr. Allen) then read a statement prepared by the Surveyor, which was to the following effect : "This sewer was commenced at Carter's House level crossing at or about the end of February, 1888, and was completed as far as Gontey-lane about the beginning of August following. All the brick walls werc built by the beginning of July. These walls were constructed in accordance with Mr. Carr's instructions, and Mr. Dux- bury informed the sub-Committee that he frequently went down to see the gas and water pipes were properly supperted. I had no clerk of work at all on this work ; in Deceenber, 1887, I asked fortwo, and the Committee only granted one, and he one of the Board's workmen. He could not attend to this work, for at that time War- rington-mad sewer, two streets adjoining the Warring- ton-road Schnels, Grenfell-st. private improvement, and the widening of Birchfield-road were all proceedint at the same time. As to 3ft. wrong in levels across the Marsh, it was in my opinion plotted wrong, making the level of the Marsh 3ft lower than it really is, which does not at all affect the level and inclination of the sewer. It is the section which is mislaid, and not the plan,and this during the time of the Town Hall decorations. At the time when the plans were made, there was a good outlet in the river, and after the work was commenced, which would be over twelve mouths, a bank had formed extending 100 yards.into the river. Mr. Campbell, who acted as clerk of works for me for a few weeks, informed me of this, and said it, was requisite to have pipes laid in the bank so as to obtain a proper outlet, and some- time previously to the work being ecnatructed under the canal and railway this bank was completely washed away. As 6 inch gulley drains in the schedule of prices are priced at 45. per yard, in my opinion ss. 6d. is not sufficient for 9 inch pine drains under the circumstances referred to. It was oriehially intended to put timber piling at the river end, and also to have a length of 27 yards of cast iron pipes with a ti dal flap thereto—but owing to the action of the tide setting in on the Lanca- shire side, after the sewer across the Marsh had been laid, this could not be done through the fretting away of the bank; in consequence of this the flap had to be placed in the manhole, and the earthenware pipes lowered to enable the flap to swing clear. Lieutenant Simpson objected to the cast iron pipes, and earthenware pipes were substituted for them. Length of the old route across the Marsh 323 yards ; length of new route across the Marsh 276 yards, and 27 yards relaid, making 303 yards according to measurement bill. Owing to the short time allowed for getting in tenders the quantities were not ready before the 25th July, 1887, and tenders had to be sent in on the 28th July, 1887, this giving the contractors only two days to make out their tenders; therefore I had no opportunity to eitmine the quantities. The whole of the contractors were informed whilst inspecting the plans that the Board would bear the cost of letting off the Canal, as it was impossible for them to estimate thecost of the same. The phrase was put in the bill of quantities without my knowledge and it was not referred to in the specification. Extra measurements have never been put on the plans. The measurements by the sub-committee should be put into varda, as follows : (1) difference 2 cubic yards, (2) difference 21 cubic yards, (3) 'difference 21 cubic yardsjotal 7. As I had no Clerk of Works 1 took the depths from the section, and omitted to take off the thickness of the flag covers, &c. Tne junctions and con- nections are in my opinion correct, and I cannot under- stand how the sub-committee arrived at their lengths of drains. The sewer had to be altered in various places to miss gas and water mains where it waspossible to do so. Had it not been so altered the cost would have been more through the mains having to be supported. Extra excavation under railway at schedule price cost £2O, and being reduced to is. Bd. per cubic yard, equals 240 cubic yards, leaving 294 cubic yards for altering line of sewer. Difference not accounted for £351. Clay puddle, £lll 6s. ; carting away excavation displaced by clay puddle and brick walls, £4B is. ' • brick walls, £lO2 ; I cement concrete, £3O 12s. 6d. ; extra depth across marsh, £49 Bs. 4d. ; flag covers, £ll ; total, £352 7s. 10d. The

delay in the account not being rendered sooner was ow- ing to so much work haying to be performed. There was no need to construct a flushing tank when the Board had purchased a portable one. The ventilating shafts mild not be erected through Mr. Bibby refusing to sell sites for the same. The length of steel tube is 118 feet. Steel and iron cost £l6l 9s. 4d., workmanship, £159 19s. 2d.; fixing Asc., £25; 483 cubic yards ex- cavation at 4s. 10d., £ll6 14s. 6d. ; total £463 3e. The price of steel tube is per lineal foot, and not per lineal yard, and is at the rate of £3 18s. 6(1. per foot. The price of steel plate was £5 10s. per ton ; the price of Low Moor iron was £2O: steel rivets and bolts and nuts, £l5. These prices have been considered reasona.bleprices. The price for excavation is the same allowed for in the Schedule as if cast iron pipe had been laid. There was very great difficulty in getting the plates owing to delay which I had no control of. The only price which seems excessive is the charge for making the tube. Additions and deductions sheets have always been furnished the Committee for evry contract when the final account has been sent in. When the line of a sewer has to be altered owing to gas and water mains, any expense in connection therewith the coatractar is entitled to, as any expense in building brickwork he would be paid for. The extra depth across the marsh is charged for in the measure- ment bill—as 593 cube yards at is. Bd. I wish to call the Board's attention to the amount of work which has been put upon'the Surveyor's Department, during the last four years in the making of public improvements, sewering, and private street improvements. A list is annexed showing them, and cost of repairs to the roads. When the present private street contracts are completed the amount expended in four years upon the same will be about £19,500. Since the time I have been here (which Ls nearly 15 years) the Board have never yet lost any- thing by private street improvements, and the difficulties in connection with the carrying out of the 150 section of the Public Health Act are very great. Since my appointment the population has increased 15,000,making now a population of 32,000, which muck necessarily mean an increase in the cost of repairs. To keep the roads in an efficient state they require constantattention. I have always tried to keep down office expenses." The list referred to was also read by the clerk. Mr. J. Taylor said that no extra work had been thrown upon the Suryeyer • they could get no informa- tion from him.—Mr. Liddell said that at almost every meeting the Surveyor had not given satisfactory explana- tions. He should not think the Surveyor should be called incompetent, but he was absolutely without methed.—Mr. Wright remarked that the Surveyor waS not alone the servant of the Highway Committee, but of the whole Board. The Health Committee and the General Purposes Committee demanded a good deal of his attention, and his time was pretty well taken up. *le thought that the Surveyor deserve() more confidence than he had had hitherto.—Mr. Carey said that want of method, and reticence, seemed to be the faults of the Surveyor, and the question was whether or not the Highway Committee could work with him.—Dr. O'Keefe considered the reply of the Surveyor an absolute refuta- tion of the charges made against him, and he himself was satisfied with it.—Mr. Cook, Mr. Handley, and Mr. Gaskell supported the action of the Committee —The recommendation of the Highway Committee, which was to the effect that the Surveyor be asked to resign, was then voted upon. Nine members voted in favour of the recommendation, which was passed, two voting against it, and other members declining to vote. This was all the business. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

div.head: PENSIONERS AND PAUPERISM.
div.p: PENSIONERS AND PAUPERISM.

The Burton-on-Trent Union had forwarded resolutions advocating that Army and Navy pensioners who were in receipt of relief from the Union, should be compelled to repay the Guardians for their maintenance. div.head: EAVY PRECEPT FROM TYE COUNTY -COUNCIL.
div.p: EAVY PRECEPT FROM TYE COUNTY -COUNCIL.

_ The Clerk said he had received a precept from the Cheshire County Council for £4,706 13s sd, to be paid 01} the first of March next.—Mr. Weir: Oh' Murder! —The Assistant Clerk said a circular letter had been sent to the overseers of the various township telling them to prepare to meetthe call.—The Clerk said some townships would not require to make a special rate as they had sufficient in hand to pay the call.—Mr. Haywood read a report the Finance Committee on the subject from which it appeared that in the present ha,II year's estimates it was estimated that the County Council would require £2036 so that theprecept was .£2670 13s. 3d. more than was ex- meted, In 1886-7 the amount paid the County w a £442195. 4d ;in 1887.8 £4398 16s id; in 1888-9 £3321 2s. id ; and for 1889-90 the amount including the pre- sent precept would be £6899 19s 7d. which was an in- crease over the previous year of £3578 159 Bd. The balance in the treasurer's hands was £2351 146 2d, hut after meeting all liabiliies including the eat! from County Council there would be a deficit of £lBlO 19s 3d.—Mr Weir: We were better off before we had &County Council—Mr Aaron: We shall be worse still. —The Chairman said the Committee had made no recommendation en the subject.—The Clerk said it was for the Board to say whether a special precept should be issued to the overseers.—Mr. Aaron : Cannot we in- sist upon the County Council giving Us particulars of what this extra money is for P—The Assistant-Clerk said' they were not, entitled to ask for more than had been supplied.—Mr. Aaron said it was unreasonable to expect the overseers to collect the money asked for in four weeks, and especially in small villages like Weston, where they had to find £l4B Ile. Id. Thank God, tan could pay the call without making a new rate, but he. was thinking of the other country townships, which were not so fortunately situated. He moved that the Clerk write and ask the County Council to defer payment of the precept until the end of April. It would be a great saving to the ratepayers of the Union.—The Assis- tant-Clerk : Y6U cannot save anything. Nothing is paid for collecting it. It comes within the assistant- overseer's duties.—Mr. Aaron: Can you expect him to make and collect a special rate for nothing, when he will get more curses over collecting this extra 4d. rate than for • collecting an ordinary shilling rate. (Laughter.)—The. Assistant Clerk stated that extra payment could only be - made for collecting a special sanitary rate. In reply to ' a question he. said the County Council had a payment of - about £l,BOO or £2,000 to make to the Runcorn Union. —Mr. Aaron suggested that the County Council should be informed that if the money was not paid by the Ist of - March the bailiffs would be sent, same as they would to -• the overseers if the ealis were not paid. (Liughter.)— - Mr. Jeffs seconded the motion to defer payment. .A. special rate would cause endless trouble and vexation in the villages, where it was more difficult to obtain money than in the towns. In Helsby they could net possibly find the money by the Ist of March. They might saY "We can make you." But it would be a month before they could make the overseers find the money so they would be no faster. (Laughter.)—The Clerk said if Mr. Aaron would write his resolution he would forward it to the County Council. He would not take any responsi- bility himself.—The Assistant Clerk said he could not see how the precept could stand over.—Mr. Speakman said the County Council was the child of the Government and they could not help themselves. They had got instructions from Government to do certain work, and - they were bound to do it and he did not think anything - would be gained by deferring this matter. Of course it seemed a great amount of money ter the Guardians to I find, brit it was a thing that could not be helped. ' The simple origin of the matter was this. The Quarter Sessions instead of levying a rate just before. they left office and their duties were transferred to the County Council, handed over a debt to the Council, and the consequence was that the Guardians were asked to pay now what they should have paid at the beginning of 1889,. so that they were not in a very much worse position only in regard to a little extra expenditure. The - main roads of the district were being taken over by the Council and there was a little extra expense= that head. The Government in former years had given about £lO,OOO per annum for County purposes on main roads, but this sum had not been given the Council this year - and would not be again. Then instead of getting . £15,000 from the Weaver Trust, the Council only received £lO,OOO. The loss of two such large sums would account . , for the extra call the Guardians had received land he did not see the slighest use in asking for the • matter to be deferred. In reply to Mr. Parr, Mr. Speak- • man explained that the contribution from the Weaver Trust had been reduced because there was not so great a demand for salt in 1889 as in previous years. He understood that at the present time. the Salt Union was very busy, and there was no doubt that the revenee would he very much increased in 1890.—1 t was sug- .gested that the Union balance should he use:l to pay the precept from the Council, but the Clerk said they could not do that: ttere would not be so large a balance at the end of the half year. Ile explained that they should only ask the town.hips for £2,600 the difference between what the Guardians estimated for and what the Coundl wanted--Mr. Haywood asked if they could not deduct from the precept the sum of £2OOO which the Council owed the Union ; and the Clerk replied in the negative. After further discussion the motion to defer payment - was passed without dissent.

div.head: DOMESTIC DIFFERENCES AT SANKEY
div.p: DOMESTIC DIFFERENCES AT SANKEY

BRIDGES. A WIFE'S "TWO YEARS' MISERY." At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs. W. F. Gooch, A. C. McCorquoclale and T. D. Grimke, Joseph Gill, described as an iron- roller, at the works of Messrs. Monks, Hall and Co., Warrington, and living at Sankey Bridges, was summoned for assaulting his wife Mary. The defendant pleaded not guilty. Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for the complainant, stated that though the summons was one for common assault he should ask the magistrates to convict the defendant of an aggra- vated assault. The parties had been married about two years, the complainant having been a widow with three or four children. At the time of the marriage she had a draper's shop in which she had made a living for herself , and children. The defendant earned something between £3 and £4 per week but was continually drunk. During the last two years the woman's life had been nothing but misery. The defendant left his work at half-past five on the morning of the 17th January, but instead of going home, which was only about 150 yards away, he went to the Coach and Horses in Liverpool-road and stopped five hours until he got thoroughly "well soaked." He came home drunk, asked his wife to get the breakfast ready and "be— quick about it." When he got it he threw it at her and charged her with misconduct with some travellers who came for orders to the shop. The defend- ant, Mr. Browne added, seemed to be going out of his mind either with drink or something else and the police were continual' 7 having to go out of their way to watch him. Later on th,, Same day he rushed at her and struck her. He continued his conduct throughout the day and at dinner time kicked over a table on which was the dinner for two of her sons. When she complained about his conduct he kicked her. He also tore a silk handker- chief from her neck and nearly strangled her and threw `the handkerchief on the fire. When she snatched it from the fire, he gave her two blows on the breast. Since the complainant had taken out the summons he had threatened what he would do to her, and, as she was afraid of her life she applied for a separation order.— Defendant: lam quite agreeable to it.—The complain- ant then gave evidence in support of Mr. Browne's state- ment, and Constable Dugdale said the wife had frequently complained to him about her husband's con- duct. He had seen her outside unable to get in the 'house.—The Bench stated that they were of opinion that the defendant had committed a very aggravated assault upon his wife, and it was a disgrace for a man to treat a woman as he had done. He would be fined 40s and costs, or in default of payment, one month's imprison- ment. Mr. Browne then applied, on behalf of the wife for a t judicial separation order. lie said that during the two years the parties had been married the defendant had made it a continual course of drunkenness and assault. On one occasion at Oxford-road station, Manchester, he attempted to throw his wife in front of a train, but two men prevented him. On Walking Day last he gave her a black eye and cut her lip open; and a fortnight ago he threw a carving knife at her. He asked the Bench to grant the separation, and to order the defendant to con- tribute 20s. or 30s. per week towards the support of his wife.—Defendant: I hope you may get your 30 " hob " per week.—The Bench subsequently made an order of separation, and ordered the defendant to contribute 15s. per week.

BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
WIFE DESERTION.

Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Conk, a man named John Grelly, was summoned for having deserted his wife on the 16th of December. Mrs. Grelly said that on the day in question her hitsbantreame home drunk, kicked up a row, and then left hole. He had returned this week. The mag,istratesordalea him to pay his wife 10s. a week. A MAN WHO I) ri AMES THE "CAT."

Robert Mulholland, of M—ersey-st., was before the War- rington magistrates on Monday on a charge of drunken- ness. After the case had been prfived, the Chief Constabe (Mr. Hunt), told the magistrates that prisoner was a dangerous man; he was one of the worst men that he (Mr. Hunt) knew.. If any man deserved the cat-o- nine tails it was the prisoner. The police of olden times, who each had a good ashplant, would have cured him. His wife, who keeps a lodging-house, paid him to keep away from her, but when he was short of money he returned anctill-used her. The magistrates imposed a fine of 10s. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment'.

div.head: DOG IN COURT.
div.p: A DOG IN COURT.

• William Whitlow, innkeeper, and farmer at Preston Brook, was summoned before the Daresbury Sessions on Tuesday, under the order recently issued for the muz2l- - of dogs. A police afficc4 stated that Mr. Whitlow allowed a dog to run about on the highway on several occasions with a strap muzzle • on which was really no muzzleSt all. The muzzle was so slack that the officer had seen the dog eating a bone on the highway. The magistrates asked if the dog was about, and Mr. Whit- low replying theat it was, it was brought into court and the bench were shown the muzzle.' ' The Bench con- sidered the strap around the dog's mouth ought to be a little tighter, but they dismissed the summons against Mr. Whitlow. The police officer referred tO another dog, but Mr. Whithw sa.id, he bad not brought it. It was fifteen years old, had not a tooth in its head, and was blind of one eye and deaf. (Laughter).

div.head: WINWICK-STREET OBSTRUCTION CASES,
div.p: THE WINWICK-STREET OBSTRUCTION CASES,

On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, Elizabeth Hallows and John Gregg appeared in answer to sum- monses charging them with obstructing the footpath in Winwick-st. by exposing thereon goods for sale.—Aldsr- man Davies observed that...the cases were adjourned in order that they might go before the Watch and Market Committees for consideration.—The Chief Constable said that the matter was mentioned at the Watch Committee meeting, and the decision come to was the same as that arrived at 'in November last.—Alderman Sutton : Did the matter go before the Market Committee ?—The Chief Constable: I don't know.—Alderman Davit* said that the Bench wanted the Committee to consider whether they could, with propriety, ajlow anything to be exposed for sale where it was so much out of the roadway. The Bench decided to fdrther• adjournthe ,cases for a fort- night, to enable the subject, to be brought before both Committees.
AN OFFICER TIIRNS Hts LANTERN ON AND A OITURIT • BOLTS. - -

P. C. Dutton, a tall young policeman stationed at Moore, was on his rounds very early on the morning of the 18th of January when he met two strange men, who afterwards gave their names as George Jackson and Joseph Shawcross. He turned his lantern upon them and Jackson, who had a bag, ran away. Dut- ton ran after him and overtook him, and on ex- amining the bag found three fowl in it. He asked the to men where they had got the fowl from, and Jackson replied that they had picked them up on the road, but Shawcross advised his companion to '6 let the b—find it out.' Dutton aftcrwards found out that

.„.„ the fowl had been stolen from the premises of Mr. W. Beswick at Walton. The two men were charged with the theft at Daresbury Sessions. on Tuesday, and as they had been extremely reticent with regard to their antece- dents the police asked for a remand, which was granted.

div.head: CHARGE 08 THEFT BY • WOM•N.
div.p: CHARGE 08 THEFT BY • WOM•N.

On Tuesday, at the Warrington Police Court, a married woman named Jane Tickle, who lives, at 8, Rodney-st., was charged with having stolen a half-sovereign, the property of John Jordan. a forgeman. From the evi- dence given it appeared that the wife of the complain- ant owed the defendant 35., which she had previously borrowed. On Saturday Mrs. Tickle called on Mrs. Jordan and asked her what. she intended to do with respect to the money that was owing to her. The prosecutor replied that she could do nothing that week, but was willing to give the defendant 6d. as interest. At that time the prosecutor held in her hand her husband's wages, which consisted of a half sovereign, a florin, a sixpence, and three penny pieces. She, on the defend- ant assenting to the proposal, as she thought, gave Mrs. Tickle a sixpence. Jordan, however, saw that his wife had given the dz•fendant the half sovereign by mistake. ;He told her, and she at once deteced the error. The defendant denied that she had received the half sovereign, but the Bench considered the case proved, and ordered her to pay a fine of 203. and costs, or in default to under- go a month's imprisonment with hard labour. She was also ordered to refund the stolen money. ROBBING CHILDREN IN THE STREETS. • •

At the Warrington Police Court,on Monday,at the close of the business, the Chief Constable said he wished be give publicity to a matter which had been engaging the attention of the police for some time past. Saturdays and Mondays were two busy days with pawnbrokers, and it was a habit in Warrington for persons who pledge goods to send children with them to the pawnbrokers. They were very careful to send children apparently of thn age of 12 years, because if a pawnbroker took any- thing from a child under that age he was liable to a penalty but they did not hesitate to send children of seven, eight, nine, or ten, to redeem the goods, and sometimes they were entrusted with as much as lie. ed., 9s. 6d., and ss. to get articles out of pawn. A number of children had recently been robbed on their way to or from the pawnbrokers, some of the amounts stolen being 10. Bd., us. 6d. and ss. Three such robberies occurred on Saturday. The police had used every possible effort to detect the thieves, but had hitherto been unsuccessful, and he thought if a little publicity was given through the medium of the Press it might have a deterrent effect, and might prevent persons from sending children of so tender an age on such errands. At Widnes several rob- beries of wages had taken place when children had been sent to fetch them, but nothing of that kind had been reported in Warrington. A GIRL BEYOND CONTROL. ' -

An elderly woman, named Rose McNally, was eharged at the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday morning-, with having assaulted her daughter, a girl Of fourteen years of age. From a statement made by the Chief Con- stable (Mr. Runt), it appeared that the parties live at 13 Navlonstreet, and that Mrs. McNally takes in washing and keeps lodgers. Complainant said that on Sunday her mother gave her some weak tea, which she refused to drink, and thereupen her mother thrashed her with a leather strap. In reply to Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for the defence, complainant admitted having run away from work at the mill, and haying tried to throw her- self into the mill pond. She also admitted having used offensive language to her mother, and having otherwise misbehaved herself. The whole of the neighbourhood had reproved her (complainant) for her bad conduct,— A witness named Smith, said that she saw defendant "jump on the complainant."—lnspiector Spinks said that after the alleged assault he examined the complain- ant, and found about ten or twelve marks on her body; her arms and the top of her shoulders were black, and great violence must have been used to produce the injuries. Three or four of the neighbours had com- plained about the,girl, but others had complained about the mother.—Mr. Browne said that the complainant had been a constant source ot trouble to her mother, to whom she constantly used disgustir.g language. The mother was compelled to use force to control the girl.— After hearing witnesses for the defence, the Bench dis- missed the ease.

Mr. Fletcher, of Northwich, appeared for the defendant. ' The prosecutor alleged that the defendant knocked him down, and the money in his pockets rolled over the pavement, and prosecutor threatened to take out a sum- mons against his employer. Leach then said that in that case he would have the shirts, and took the bundle i from 'him. Prosecutor stayed in the "yaddy-house " until morning, when he mentioned the matter to P.C. Harrison. For three weeks he "walked along the roads starving." Mr. Fletcher addressed the magistrates for the defence, and said that, finding Donoghue had been paid for more work than he had done, defendant asked for several shillings back. Donoghue felt to the ground, but gave up the shirts as security for the money owing. Mr. Pierpeint said that although the Bench dis- missed the case, he could not help saying that Mr. Leach had acted in an unjustifiable manner. He had no right to assault Donoghue, nor to take the shirts as security, because security was not to be obtained by force. Mr. Fletcher said he had applied for a warrant for perjury, but he admitted there was difficulty in the case, as an indictment for perjury required cerrobora- tion.—The case was then disrmssed. GAMEKEEPHRS USE THEIR Szrcxs.—Themas Swift and John Crank were charged with night poaching at Dares- bury, on the 15th inst., on land in theoccupation of Thos: Weir.—Joseph Jones, keeper for Sir Richard Brooke, stated that on the morning in question at 2.30, in company I with about a dozen other watchers, he was on Mr. Weir's land, when they saw the defendants in the act of poach- ing. They had a bag with them which contained three rabbits, and an empty bag was found in the possession of Crank. They also found some sticks (now produced) on the ground, which he believed belonged to the poachers. In answer to Mr. Percy Davies, who appeared for the defence, witness said the prisoners did not resist being Apprehended. They received blows from some of the keepers, but he did not know who they were, er why they had received such treatment.—George Rigby, under- gamekeeper for Sir Richard Brooke, said he was in com- pany of the last witness, and he apprehended the prisoner Crank, and left him in the custody of a watcher of the name of Rowlinson, and followed Swift and brought him back to Crank, and he found that in his absence some- one had pushed a sharp-pointed stick into the mouth of Rowlinson, but he did not see any blood, but the next day the man's lip was swollen. -By Mr Davies: He did not hear Rowlinson complain Until* next day, and he did not see any blood on Rowlinson's face. Witness admitted striking the prisoner Crank, as he thought he had better get the first blow. Crank did not resist in any way.—Swift was sent to prison for a month : Crank was fined 405., and costs and bound over to keep the peace for six months, himself in £lO and one surety of £s.—Mr. Pierpoint (addressing the keepers) : Game- keepers should boa little more careful as t o the way they use the heavy sticks now produced. L think , know how the whole thing happened.. You thought these defendants were going to hit you, probabiy they were, but you hit them. There should, however, be moderation in everything. Don't hit quite so hard. If you see an absolute necessity to hit, you must use your judgment as to how far you should go i I don't think that Swift got very severely injured, but Crank got a severe blow on his head.

A woman, named Pearce, has been arrested at Bir- mingham charged on suspicion with having caused the death of a gentleman. named Toog,ood. They drove in a cab on Wednesday from Walsall to Birmingham, and Toogood died a few minutes after leaving the woman. Poisoning is suspected.

After several days' inquiry into the cause of the death of the 64 men and boys who met with their death by an explosion at the Moss&ld Colliery, Longton, in ,October last, the inquest concluded on Thursday. After an hour and a half's deliberation, the following verdict was returned :---That death was caused by explosion, but there was no evidence to show how it was caused. They tound that the manager was not guilty of culpable negligence in not withdrawing the men from the mine on the night of October 15th, but they added a rider that he was deserving of censure for not inspecting the mine for so long a time previous to the explosion. Jolley was of considerable advantage but the Rangers, headfid.by Pickard and Nowell, rushed down the field, ad were only checkii'd by Sampsoa making a difficult catch; which ingiilted in the ball being sent- to mid. field. Give-and-take play followed, and then Daniels dodged to mid-field. Wall next threw well across to Adams, whoge kick too'k play to the visitors' gararters, , and after Mather had repeatedly stopped his opponents' ' rushes, Lawless got finally away, only to see I.)* pus intercepted, and the ball taken back., Ultimately, a splendid dribble, started by Thorniley,Berry, and Davies, was the means of play being taken under the Rangers' pats. The home forwards, who seemed much smarter than the visiting front rank, soon relieved, and a long , kick sent. the ,ball into touch at the Warrington quarter r flag, where a series of packed anil loose scrimmages monopolized the game for a lengthy' period. Berry,.R. Barnes, and Isherwood, however, got the ball awayrand a rattling bit of play by Lawless and Sampson was next witnessed. A lot of uninteresting scrim- mages followed, but Wall finally ran the ball to his opponents' territory. Warrington then screwed a scrimmage finely, and a good bit of play by A. Barnes and Howarth neutralized. Subsequently, the home team dribbled over the line, and a lengthy maul ensued, Lawless securing the verdict, and only a minor obtained. Following the dropout Neild and M'olyneux shone by good work and then Thornley and Davies started a rush at midfield, and when half-time arrived the Rangers had secured one minor to nil. Restarting against the wind, the home teain at once pressed, and Warrington had all their work cut out to keep their opponents from scoring, Davies and R. Barnes doing some rare tackling. After a lot of packs the ball was rushed by Molyrieux. Neild, and Isherwood to neutral territory, and a long kick by , Jolley forced the home team to defend. •A rush by Oman, Shaughnessy, and Dalton carried play to the visi- tors' 25, and Warrington were pressed umtil a kick by Mather relieved. Ultimately after some loose scrambling play Berry secured at midfield and ran grandly along touch and threw to Thornley, who repassed to Daniels, the latter scoring a try, and although the place was extremely difficult Isherwood only just failed to land the premier point. Succeeding the drop out the Rangers rushed away, but Jolley stopped the rush, and then , Daniels made a lot of headway by a run and kick. For some time the home team were pressed, but when relief came Roberts and Wall by a pretty piece of passing transferred to midfield, this being suppleinented by a strong run by Corns, who' when looking extremely dan- gerous, was grandly floored by Sampson The succeed- ing play was uninteresting,the game ending in a win for Warrington by one try to one minor. YORKSHIItii v. CITESHIRg. The Committee of the Cheshire Union met on Monday evening, at the Albion Hotel, Manchester; and selected the following fifteen to play against Yorkshire, on Saturday week, at Birken- head: J. W Brazendale (Runcorn), back ; J. T.. Has- lain (Dukinteld), J. H. Crompton (Runcorn), and F. P. Jones (New Brighton), three-quarters ; H. Hughes (Run- corn) and F. W. Spence (Birkenhead Park), half backs; A. G. Wood and.P.,H. Lockwood (Birkenhead Park), W. Faulkner, W. Hughes, P. Riley, W. F. Hancock, and R. Dolan (Runcorn), C. Schofield (Stockport), and W. A. Williams (New Brighton), forwards. FRODSHAM Y. ST. MART'S, WiDNE.9.—These teams met at Frodsham, on Saturday, St. Mary's kicked off', a gusty and unpleasant wind bitiwing at the time. Frod- sham defended in capital styleri.and play was confined to the Centre for come time. St. Mary's were compelled to touch down, and on the kick-out Frodsham were con- fined to close quarters. Clough put in the saving clause .by neatly dribbling. A scrimmage ultimately ensued, and the ball was forced off the line, and Whelan scored a try. Frodsham in the second half showed up better, and the visitors' territory was the scene of hostilities for some time, until Whalley, who neatly passed, equalized matters, but the kick at goal failed. Far the home team Rogers. Clough, Darlington, and Lightfpot played well, whilst Whelan was the pick of the visitors. Score: Frodsham, 1 try., 2 minors ; Widnes St Mary's, / try, 3 minors.

ST. HBLENS RECRBA.TION T. FIOLI3ECV.—The St. Helens Recs. visited Holbeck Recreation Groisnds, on Saturday, when they encountered Holbeck. The weather was boisterous, but three thousand people attended. The I wind blew almost a hurricane, and the two captains agreed to divide the game into four qizarters. The toss having been won by the visitors, who• played with the wind Gerrard With a flying kick sent the ball well into the home " 25," where Seddon landed it over the bar, the point tieing disallowed for some infringement. The home forwards put in some good work. Liversedge securing a try, which North failed to convert. The second quarter- was entered upon, and scrimmages on the visitors line ensued, from which Wilson scored a try, North again failing. In the third quarter the visitors pressed haed and made a determined onslaught on the home citadel,. their efforts being rewarded by Ellison getting over, but Seddon failed at goal. In the last quarter the visitors played up most determinedly, and for a time the home goal was in jeopardy. Holbeck were the winners of the tough match by two tries and one minor to one try and one minor. Sr. Hermsm v. LElGH.—Great interest was taken in this West Lancashire League match, at St. Helens, on Saturday. There were from 4,000 to 500 spectators present, amongst whom was Mr. Seton-Karr, M.P. Teams: St Helens: Goulding, full back; Sudlow, Fair dough, and Foreman, threequarters ; Cross and Little,. half backs ; Dearden, Graham, Borthwick, Twist, Flynn . Hardman alton, and the two Brownbint, - forwards: Leigh; ea Hop,-full back; Worthington, Smith, Forrest, three-quarters; Gormon and Shovelton, half backs ; Pendlebury, Higgins, James Pecullebury, Isaac Taylor, P. Taylor, McMaster, Glynn, Dawson, and Rawson, for-- wards. The visitors played one man short until nearly half time.. Smith, the Leigh captain, kicked off against the wind, and the ball being at once returned past the forward opponents, Tom Coop was called upon to save, which he did by kicking out of play. The home team kept up the pressure, and Fairclowsh made his mark in a good position, but the attempt to improve was a miser- able one. The play was fast, and in favour of- tho homesters ; who on two or three occasions had very bard lines in not scoring. The game was divided Into four quarters and in the second period Hardmarso Sudlow. Fairclongh, and Cross played well for the /mine team. Just before the close the wind baffled the home team, and Leigh managed to get a lucky try the. goal' kick entrusted to Coop being successful. ,The Saints played op well, and although they could not score themselves, they fought well against the wind, and the visitors only obtained another minor. The final result wasa win for Leigh by nine points to one, the score being Leigh, one goal and one minor ; St. Helens, one minor. ,

SALE V. RUNCORN.—There is always a great amount of interest in Sale attached to the fixture of the home team 1 with Runcorn, and on Saturday, when the two teams met on the Brooklands ground, they were faced by a large number of spectators. . The teamsweee as, follows: —Sale: E. Harvey, back; W. Stephens, and, Siddelly, threequarter backs; F. Drinkwater and 11..5. Thorpe, half-backs; T. bings, J. H. Ogden, P. H. Hooker, H. Her- vey ' , E. W. Hunt, H. Walton H. A. Howes, and C. chap- man, forwards. . linncorn : Houghton, back.:: T Crompton, S W Hughes, three-quarter backs ;.EVans and Abrahams, half-backs ; Broady, Gayter,.Lee,. Hulse, C. Hughes, Stubbs, Williams, Davies anti Andrew,,forwards. Broady started the ball fer Runcorn, and t the. kick being charged dawn, the Sale forwards rushed thetball 'down to the visitors' line. Amaul. 'ensued, hi which F. Drink- water got the best of it, and obtained a.tryforSaie about a minute from the commencement, amidst great excite- ment. The place kick was a difficult one, .and Howes failed to improve. The Sale forwards pressed severely and forced the visitors to touch downs Thorpe placed another minor to the credit of Sale by a,fine- kick. Run- corn's kick out was charged .down.by. Hunt, and a third minor resulted. Sale continued to have the better of the play, and IV. Stephens put in some neat play, and had hard lines in not getting over. Abrahams got the leather away nicely from the seriminage,and some fine play by Chapman and HrLings carried hostilities in the Runcorn quarters once again. TDavles-at length.get in possession and went away at a rattling pace, but wasbrought down by Siddelly and Harveybear theffine. E. Harley returned the ball with an equally smart piece of work. Run- now had a look in, and Crompton tried a drop at goal The leather went wide, and a rush. by Howes and H. Har- vey resulted in another, mines, for Dales After some play in the mid-field. Mr. T. Davies. again treated the spectators to a magnificent display. He was successfully tackled and nothing resulted. When. the whistle blew for half-time, the score stood, one try and four minors to 1 nothing in favour of Sale.. Runcorn had the wind in their favour in the second half,, but Sale played up with remarkable vigour. Howes kicked off with a magnificent kick, and rushing down alMdst scored a try. Houghton just managed to drop on the ball in time, and a minor resulted. Sale were then placed on the defensive, and after some combined play Abrahams passed to Gayter, who obtained the first try for Runcorn. Crompton's place kick was chae,ged down by Hunt. Sale had to concede another miaor, the passing amongst the Runcorn backsbeing admirable. Crompton gave T. Davies a neat pass, which he took advantage of and ran in a try, Crompton failing to improve. Runcorn attacked with renewed vigour, and W. Hughes took a pass from Cromp- ton in capital style, ' but Chapman tackled well and brought-his opponent to grass. Immediately afterwards, after corns judicious passing took place between Abrar hams, Crompton, and W. Hughes, and the latter got over, Crompton's kick being futile. Runcorn are riw having OM better of the game, and just before the call of J time T.. Davies broke away again, and putting on a , splendid spurt evaded the Sale backs, placing the ball behind the posts. This was looked upon as a certain goat. Crompton placed the ball nicely over the pbsts, but not before Hunt had touched it. The return fixtures between the above clubs was decided at Wilderspool on Saturday in the presence of three thousand persons. The first meeting this season had resulted in a drawn game, greatly in favour of Warringtomalthough on that occasion they failed to place a strong team in the field. With the exception of Fair Turner and Nevins, a representative team was placed in thefield cn Saturday, whilst on the other hand Moyle was away from the Rangers. The day was spring-like, the sun shining the whole of the afternoon, but a high wind prevailed, and accurate passing was thus rendered a difficulty. Massey, as captain of Warrington, won the toss, and elected to defend the pavilion goal.

By short dribbles, play was taken to the Warrington quarters, hut the movement was checked by Readies, who kicked in touch, near the half-way flag. Play was contested here for a brief period, until, by the aid of short rushes, Evans was forced to concede a minor. This unexpected form of the Rangers against the strong wind was evidently not relished by the home supporters, who called for renewed exertions. Their wishes were complied with, for a long drophy Frank Turner was mulled by Quinney, and the Broughton goal was en- dangered. Some exciting loose play here followed, the oval travelling to Evans, who essayed' to get through, but finding his career blocked, he threw across to Massey, who sprinted finely along touch, and clear- tng (ininney gained a line try,, Frank Turner's kick at goal going wide of the mark. Some neat passing by ate, Antrobus, and Barnes again, caused an attack on the railway goal, and although the Rangers were allowed a free kick, presumably for their own offensive tactics, the Warringtonians still kept on ths aggressive. Barnes now made an effort to get in,. but 09 grounding the oval he was collared. After a somewhat lengthened maul he succeeded in :wrestling the oval frail his op- ponent's grasp, but through somednfringement the point was disallowed, a minor only awarded. Exciting play ' followed in the Rangers' ground, and play rarely passed the quarter flag. Holmes' chanted a kick by Moxton, and Kennedy luckily saved. Warrington brake away on numerous occasions, and allavith a like result, the 'fatal whistle checking their onward career. After Dillon and Randles had experienced hard lines Frank Turner put in a fine sprint from a line out, and succeeded in gaining a brilliant try. He eesaaed the kick at goal, and from a difficult angle was successful, the ball striking the posts and going over- the bar. The restart was responded to by Antrobosa whose kick was well followed up by Eyres, a return being prevented. Again play was at the Rangers' end, mad after a period of desul- tory play, Lawless enlivened the proceedings by racing over the line after some neat passing by Antrobus and Bate. Frank Turner made another good lad for goal. A minor followed from Este:us reply to the drop- out. Frank Turner again became dangerous with a neat dribble, being held near, the posts, half time being called with the score—Warrington, one goal, two tries, three miners : Rangers, one minpr. The game. so ,far had been anythiag but a pleasant one. The tactics of the visitors being severely criticised by the excited arasemblage, Frank Turner re-started from midfield, and Warrington again made :a sheep attack. Eyres and Donohue became conspicuous with seine smart tackling, and from a pack close tethe half way flag Antrobus dodged Edge, mid' racing away he finally threw to Barnes, who ran and' trausfered to Lawless, the last-named being k-nocked, inta, touch close to the line. A wide pass to Massey was foiled by the smart following up of Skidmore-and Fitbanaand the half way flag was reached. Bate, saved a rush of the visiting front rank, but Littlewood neutralised by a strong run, his final pass, however, net being taken. Antrobus re- peatedly put in some graud runs, and although Barnes made a gallant bid for the premier honours on one occa- sion, the tackling was too effective; abd at times appa- , re:any too severe, to allow, of a. try being scored. By .aezaees the Rangers worked the oval to the Warrington , end, and a rare chance was given Kennedy, but he was slow in taking it, Warrington. relievieg. The Rangers returned to the attack, arid Povey, Barnes, and. Lawless changed the venue of' the quarter flag, a free kick taken by Wheeler 'sending theball dead. Soon after the drop out, Randles pet in a fine piece of work from a line, but again the wind spoiled a chance of scoring and from a pack near the halfway flag, Bate threw wide to Massey, who snapped up the chan e, and finally placed the oral, near The posts, enabling Frank TUITIPT to place a second goal:. Warrington still attacked, aed although Antrabue and Bate passed neatly Edge made no mistake this time, flooring the first-named before he could get clear. Some mart passing by Evans, Antrobus, and Massey was negatived by Higginbotham and Shaughnessey: The Rangers made extra efforts to- wer& the close to score a tangible point, but the fine tackling of Barnes prevented them, and the Warring- tonia,ns retired' adders by two, goals, two tries, threel minors to the4tangersthree minors. That the beet teatn won there was not the least doubt, and had the visitors adopted the open tactics in the first half that- occurred' th the second portion of the game, the defeat would certainly have been a greater ene than was really the case, Antrobus, Bate, Lawless, and Massey were the pick of the Warrington babas, whilst in the ferwarda Donohue, Randles, Littlewned, and FranlaTurner were the pick. The Rangers' play, dn the whole, had a strong tendency to border on rough- ness, but those who. claim attention for what smart play was showtake their ranks are Skidmore, aferst, and Menne,

Teams—Warrington. Evans, back; Massey, Barnes, and La,wless, three-quarters; Antrobus and Bate,- half backs; Frank Turner, W. Dillon, Handles, Littiewoodi Donohue, Fovey,.Eyres, and Holmes, forwards. Brough- ton Rangers : Quinney, back; Hurst, Kenroaly, ,and, Gresty-, three-quarters; Higginbotham and Edge, half -backs Mozon„ Skidmore, Fitton, Shaughnesser, Halt,, Wheediri Jackson, Squires, and Longworth,, fOrwards. Referee, Mr. I. Hunter, Birch.

WIDNES v. TYLDESLEY. —The return League conipeti- firm, between these two clubs was played at Wtinee on Saturday, before a fair number of spectators. The home teara was badly constituted, Clarke, Ga,ndy, and Stubbs being unable to play owing to ilhiess. Phimpton again took his place in the team as three- quarter. Parkinson started the leather against a strong wind, kicking out of touch in the visitors' (porters. The borne team Was at once called upon to defend, ;which they did grandly. Shaw made his mark beyond the centre tine, but his effortat goal, even withthe wind, proved fruitless. From the drop out Tyldesley again put the hotne team on the defensive, and from a scrimmage on the line a second placc, kick was awarded to them, which was of no avail. Morrisand,Parkinson were next conspicuous with some good play,. which transferred operations to the visitors' quarters, and from some loose play which followed Bury took drop kick, which failed to pass between the posts. A return from Hartles was received by Fearnley, who dodged through the home' forwards and registered the first try. Shaw took the place kick, which was successful,. From the kick off and after some good passing by the visitors Shaw again crossed the line, but the attempt at goal failed. The whistle at this point sounded for half-time, when the score was Tyldesley one goal and one try to Widnes nil. , On crossing over Widnes had slightly the advantage of their opponents, but the reckless and Uncombined play ' of some of the forwaxds neutralized all their efforts. The ball was carried from MG Qncie the Aeld to the

other in rapid succession, and no feature worthy of note occurred until the last five minutes, when Laws having got possession rushed through his Opponents and grountled the ball over the lice: The try thus obtained was by tire decision of the referee not allowed. After some even play in the centre Alligen stopped a rush by the opposing forwards but for a few minutes the-visitors continued to press. From a scrimmage in the Witton quarters Shaw added a third goal, and, after some good play by Shaw, Sid- deley. and MOrris, Thompson put on the fourth goal. The home team kept up the pressure for some minutes, until the visitors' right wing rushed up the field. Lancashire and Cheshire had varying fortunes in their matches on Saturday, -Lancashire just winning against Durham by a try and -one, minor, to four minors, 'while Northumberland vanquished Cheshire by two goals and try, to one goal, one try, and four minors. The Cheshire team was not so strong a* the one originally selected, amongst the absentees. being Crompton. The speedy Runcorn three-quarter WAS* a great loss, and had ,he been present the fortune of the game might easily have been changed. , To`-day's match between Warrington and Swinton will, unfortunately, be shorn of some of its attraction by the fact that Valentine, the famous Swinton three-quarter, and Bumby, the half back,, have been selected to do battle for the North against the South. But, even with these i'vro away, the Swintonteam still contains a large' quota of county players and will take a lot of beating. Besides the two Swinton cracks, Lancashire supplies other two players to the Northern team, namely, F Ides and Kent from Salford.

In addition to the meeting,of the Warrington and Exeter Hall gymnasts in thee National Challenge Shield' competition, other teams brought off their ties on Satur- day. Liverpool and Newport contested at the Liverpool Gymnasium, on S.turday, and Liverpool won by a total at 296 points, against 251. i Aberdeen also beat Glasgow by the large total of glet to 224 k The victory of War- rington over Exeter Hall was a very creditable affair, considering that the local gymnasium is oiily beginning its second season, while their opponents were "old hands" at the work.

GREAT FIRE AT AELFAST.

The large five-storey warehouse of Messrs. Glendin- ning and M'Leish, linen and cambric manufacturers, Belfast, was 'completely gutted by fire on Saturday night. The damage is estimated at over £.30,000. DEATH OF DR. WITHEROW. The Rev. Dr. Witherow, profeasor of Church history- and pastoral theology at Magee Cbllege,. Londonderry, died on Saturday. at the age of sixty-five years. He was distingahshed in the literature 01 the Presbyterian Church, and had written several works of great interest. THE ARMAGH RAILWAY DISASTER.

A. carpenter and contractor,,.named Isaac Johnson, who was injured in the Armagh railway disaster in June last, has been awarded £1,500 tompensation and costs from the Great Northern Railway Company of Ireland. Thomas Mann, son of Robert Mum, spirit dealer, who was also injured, has been awarded £l,ooo' with costs. INTERRUPTING A FUNERAL- _ _

----- The "Freeman's Journal" protests against the insult offered by the police to the remains of Michael O'Dwyer, ex-Town Obrprnissioner of Tipperary and secretary of the National League branch, by breaking armed into the funeral procession, forcing their way to, the graveside, and threateningly parading round the church. The re- porter, describing the scene at the grave, states that Mr. O'Brien, M.P. addressed 'a, group, of mourners at the graveside, and said he dare not trftst himself to speak on th& action of the polite, but fuve nights hence he would, be speaking to thousands ot honest English- men about it.

November, and unlawfully- removing hay, &c., from lands 'of an evicted tenant named Luke Farrell, of which Lord Annally is landlord. Luke Farrell was sen- tenced to- twenty-one days'Ampriscurrnent with hard labour. and the-other nine defendants to 14. days. ME. SMITH-BARRY AND Dit. TANNER. M.P., was concluded, !at Douglas Petty Sessions, near Cork,. on Tuesday.- The magistrates ordered Dr. Tanner to be of good behaviour.,. land to,keep the peace for twelve months by hnding, two sureties, of £lOO each, otherwise to go to prison for- I three months. The Court.-however, consented to state a case tOr the superior courts, and- on this understand- ing De. Tanner entered into the necessary recognisances.

SHOCKING TRAGEDY NEAR LIVERPOOL.

At the County Police Court, Liverpool, on Saturday, John Bell, a powerfully built negro, was zharged with having,caused the death of Catherine Finegan, a aidow, aged about fifty, at West Derbv,nea.r Liverpool. It was stated that the prisoner and the deceased had been seen together in th 6 locality one night last week, and next day the body of the woman was found in a field. A medical examination showed that the deceased had been ontraged with great violence, and that this was prob- ably the cause of death. Prisoner was remanded for a week. The inquest concluded on Tuesday. Dr. Pitts ' deposed that he had made, in conjunction with Dr. Hall, post-mortem examination of the body and had found Ulm it was in a very poor condition. From the evidence he had heard, and the appearance of the body, he was bf opinion that tho woman was intoxicated, outraged, and eft either dead from syncope or in such an exhausted condition, that death occurred from exposure to the wet and cold. There were a number of bruises on her face, legs. &c., which had the appearance or • having been I caused in a struggle between her and some other person. ?r. Ben Hall corroborated the last witness's statements. The jury returned a verdict of manslaughter against John who was accordingly committed to take his trial on this charge at the next assizes.
THE REV F. L. GOOD AND THE ENGLISH CHURCH UNION.

On Monday evening the Rev. F. L. Good gave a lecture in the schoolroom over Arpley Station, on the subject, " The English Church Union a Romaniz- log Confederacy." The chair was occupied by Mr. T. Harborne. The Rev. F. L. Good said he had from time to titue noticed that the English Church Union had held meatings in Warrington, and a short time before the advent of the Rector he saw an announcement to the effect that the English Church Union contemplated giving up the society altogether owing to lack of sympathy and support. The Union had however, since the arrival of the clergyman to whom he had referred, received an iropetus. He knew something about the working of the English Church Union, and lie was satisfied that the majority of Church going people believed it to be a society which had for its object the njaintenance of the doctrines of the Church of England, and which was determined to prevent error creeping into it. But that was not the case. The English Church Union opposed Protestantism ..and reviled the reformers and the Reformation. The late Rey. A. H. Mackonochie publicly stag- Matized Protestantism as "A cold, miserable, unlov- unchrist-like, godless figment," while in his lecture delivered at Liverpool before the _4l:!filish Church Union in April, 1868, Dr. Littledale, a °Qegate of the Union, grossly vilified the Protestant re- formers and martyrs by remarking "A Church which Could produce in its highest lay and clerical ranks such a set of miscreants as the leading English and Scottish reformers, must have been in a perfectly rotten state, 12:5 rotten as France was when the righteous judgment of Pg great revolution fell upon it." Mr. Good also con- ed that the party press reviled the Reformation, and that the English Church Union upheld the doctrine that ne clergy were sacrificitig priests and the confessional, and shielded confessionalists. Mr. Gdod further con- thatf the Union dethroned the Bible to exalt the Church "tradition" and the crucifix, that it incul- cated Praying for the dead ; favoured image worship and Mariolatry, which was steadily finding its place 31,i the literature and churches of the Ritualists. t here was a branch of the English Church in Warring- If the branch had few clerical members it had taarlY sympathisers among the local clergy. From time te time reports of its meetings appearea in the local PaPero, and at one meeting, when the Bishop of the dio- rae (Dr. Ityle) was openly assailed and spoken of most blreePectfully, most of the local clergy were present, ut not one Of them had the manliness to stand up and rebuke the speaker. If the clergy of Warrington were not all members of the Union they had attended the Meetings ,A the branch, and it wascommonly said, "Tell :le what company you keep and I will tell you what you In conclusion,. he wished to remind them that ',ere was in Warrington a branch of the Reformed _march of England, in which Protestants could honour u‘od as their fathers had done, where "crosses," so-called '-altars," "father-confessors," and Romish teaching were u.nknown, and where the Gospel was. preached and the tights and liberties of its membersrespected. (Applause.) -1:;:Mr. GALLOWAY, in proposing a vote of thanks to the 'ear for his lecture, said there was a necessity not only a„r a Reformed Church in Warrington. but for one in tverY parish throughout the United Kingdom. (Hear, car.)—Mr. Joawsox seconded the motion, which was ftrtied, after which a vote of thanks was accorded the , bairman, on the motion of Mr. GANDY, seconded by Mr. BTowrrt-E, and the meeting was brought to a conclusion,

MORRIS BROOK MECHANICS' INSTITUTE,
THELWALL.

Sir,—l thank you for your very excellent report of the opening of our Institute on the stormy night of last Tuesday. Your readers will be pleased to know that the provision made for our workmen is much appreciated by them. This is shown in the increasing numbers who attend day and night. Our Library, however, is but small, and far below the wants of our men, and it would be a source of much pleasure to our Committee if some of your kind readers would forward to me about 200 volumes suitable to men engaged on public works. I may add that the Institute is held on the Coffee Tavern premises, and visitors, as well as workmen, will find here all the accommodation they require up to 300 or 400.-1 am, Sir, yours faithfully, G. MANNING, Secretary anFl Librarian. Thelwell, Jan. 28th, 1890.

A FEB' QUESTIONS TO ROBERT FOULKES. Sir,—l noticed in last week's " Examiner " a letter from Robert Foulkes who seems never to tire' of writing about the Church, Bishop, Parsons, and things of a simi- lar character. Now I would like to call his attention to an extract from "Reynolds' Newspaper" of last week, in which the Vicar of Lockington is reported to have

-- - said, when replying to the toast of "the Bishops and Clergy of the Diocese," that he had received a message from hell to the following effect : Says the Devil—the Dlace is as full as can be ; But I'll try to make room if I can ; So let Ananias and Judas go free, And take in the Grand Old Man. Now, Robert, how is this for High Church, Low Church, Broad Church, or any other sort of Church? That is what I want to know, and, while you are about it, you might tell us, while this parson belongs to a church which claims Apostolic succession as one of its creeds, "what price you are offering Charles Peace." Last week you wrote—" Issichar is an ass," and the people green, (beg pardon) grass; not much of a mistake i though—it s the same colour—green • all of which was highly interesting, and very easy to be understood. Tell us some more of what Bishops say. The people are always anxious to hear it; they have done so much for them in the past. Bishops are men who receive enormous salaries for doing us no—l mean doing—Oh, well, I'll give it up. What are they doing ? Robert knows what they are doing, and perhaps he will inform us.-I remain, &c.,
SAMOFITNEDE.

SERIOUS C9ARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN YOUNG MAN. At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Major Hazlehurst, and Mr. G. L. Wigg. William Frederick Hancock, a fitter, in the employ of the Runcorn Waterworks Company, was charged with attempting to feloniously assault Maria Barker, 19 years of age, daughter of Mary Ann Barker of the Ferry Hotel, Church-st. Mr. A. Linaker appeared for the defence.—lt appears that Hancock lodged at the house of Mrs. Bancroft. who keeps a tobacconist shop in Church-st. On Wednesday evening, Mrs. Bancroft was attending the Co-operative Ball, and it was alleged that during her absence the prisoner invited the girl into the house, and she entered. He then called her upstairs and at length she went and the prisoner then committed the offence complained of. It was stated that Dr. McDougall was in attend- ance on the girl, who was too ill to attend the court. —The prisoner was accordingly remanded until Tuesday. Mr. Linaker applied for bail. The prisoner, he said, was a respectable young fellow, ' and he had a good defence to the charge. He was prepared to find substantial baiL—The magistrates said it was too serious a case to admit the prisoner to bail.—ln the course of the proceedings, it was stated that Hancock had arranged to be married on next Wednesday week.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. • TrURSDAY.—Before Messrs. E. K. Muspratt (chairman) and T. Sutton Timmis. MISCELLANEOUS OFFENCES —A number of parsons were each fined 6d. and costs for failing to send their children to school regularly ; some for drunkenness; some for •er • having their chimneys on fire; and others again for hay- ing their dogs at large. A WARNING TO LADS IN WEST BANK.—Thomas Mutch (15) and James Mutch 0.3), residing at Widnes, were each summoned for causing wilful damage to a bound- ary wall of West Bank School, the property of the Wid- nes School Board.—The defendants were each ordered to pay 6d and costs, and to pay' 6th for damage done to the wall.

INQUESTS Ar WIDNES. Yesterday morning, Mr. Samuel Brighouse, the County Coroner, held inquests at Widnes on the following cases: CRUSHED TO DEATH. On the 23rd January, Richard Harrison, 77 years of age, whose home was at 16, Bank-st., was killed at the works of Messrs. Mathieson and Co. He was employed greasing the wheels of a number of wagons and was attempting to pass through an opening when the engine started, and his chest was terribly crushed between the buffers. He was conveyed to the Accident Hospital and attended by Dr. McLennon . He died on the 28th Jan., from the injuries. A verdict of 'accidental death was returned.

FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS. A labourer named James Brown, went to bed about ten o'clock, on Tuesday night, at his lodgings, the Man- chester Beerhouse, Wellington-st. A few minutes after- wards he was heard descending the stairs, and after- wards to fall heavily to the bottom. He was picked up bleeding from a terrible wound on the head and in ten minutes he died. Dr. Saul said the base of the skull was fractured and the main artery severed. A verdict of accidental death was recorded. SCALDED TO DEATH BY COCOA. George Hardy, aged 15 months, son of Joseph Hardy, signalman, 7, Latham-st., died on Wednesday, from the effects of scalds received on the 14th January. On the night of that day, Mrs. Hardy was making cocoa for supper in a can. She poured some waterin the can,which she placed on the table, and while she was placing the kettle on the hob, the tray overturned the can, and the child was severely scalded on the left arm. He had since been attended by Dr. MacLennan, and death occurred as stated. The jury recorded a verdict of accidental death. SAD SUDDEN DEATH. Mrs. Barrett, of Alforde-St., Widnes, about 8 o'clock on Tuesday morning, found her daughter Ellen lying in bed in an undonscious state. She remained in that con- dition until nine o'clock when she expired. - As the girl was seven years of age, and had enjoyed the best of health all her life, the Coroner ordered a post-mortem examination. Dr. MacLennan had made the necessary examination and deposed that death was due to convul- sions. Verdict accordingly.

PENKETEI. BAND OF HOPE MEMING. A Band of Hope meeting was held in the Pen- keth Day School, Mr. Naylor, of Thelwall, in the chair, on last night week. The programme was gone through in a pleasing manner by the choir, Yias Hobson, Miss Cook, Miss Watson, Miss Ashton, Mr Greenbalgh, Mr. J. smith, Miss A. Moses and Miss Mabel Garnett. The meeting was a success and the proceeds were in aid of .Mr. Stephenson's Orphanage.

SCIIOOL TREAT. On Thursday evening the junior scholars of St. Mary's, Great Sankey, and the Penketh Mission Sunday Schools. had their annual treat. About 300 children sat down to tea, after which Mr. Thos. Owen treated them to some views by the aid of a magic lantern. The ladies of the church had sup- plied a large Christmas tree, which was loaded with toys and illuminated. At the close each child had some toy given to it and the little ones gave three hearty cheers for the ladies and gentlemen who had so kindly officiated at the entertainments. Last evening the elder scholars had their treat; 250 sat down to a substantial tea, and lifter tea an interest- ing programme was gone through. INTERESTING PRESENTATION. An interesting ceremony was performed at the Works of the Peaketh Tannery Co. Limited, last

night week. Mr. James Cheetham the oldest work- man in the employ of the company, presented on behalf of his fellow workmen a splendid black marble timepiece, to Mr. George Randall, who is leaving the service of the Tannery Co. to take charge of one of the London yards of Messrs. S. Barrow and Bro. Mr. Cheetham said Mr. Randall had been with them for about eight years and they trusted he would be successful in his new situation., Mr. Randall, in reply, expressed his thanks for the present and said he accepted it in the spirit it was given. Mr. C. E Parker, managing directtr, on behalf of the company expressed their regret that Mr. Randall was leaving and said he had been a good servant and his services were appreciated. He left with their best wishes for his future welfare. Apart from the Tannery, Mr. Randall, since he came into the neighbourhood, has done a good and active service in the interests of the Liberal Club and of the Penketh Mutual Improvement Association, of which he was secretary.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

SPECIAL Missmx.—During the week there hall been a miision held in connection with the Primitive Methodist Chapel. and the meetings held have been well attended. BAND OF HOPE ENTERTAINMENT.—In connection with the Congregational Band a Hope Society, a magic lan- tern exhibition was given in the schoolroom on Monday evening. There was a good attendance. The views depicted illustrated a visit to Wales, Scotland, and Ire- land; also a temperance story was represented, and the entertainment concluded by a series of comic slides being shown.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

UNION CirIIRCH.—On Wednesday evening the annual meeting on behalf of foreign missions was held in the Union Church, Frodsharn, under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Rigby, of Sutton Weaver. The Rev. Mr. Ellison, a returned missionary from India, was the deputation. After a short address by the Chairman, Mr. Harry Turton read a list of the subscriptions received during the year, from which it appeared that the total amounted to £l4 3s. lid. After the deputation had spoken on mission work in India, a short account of the Baptist Missionary and the London Missionary Societies was given by the Rev. J. Dyer Bray. The collections at the close amounted to £1 19s. 9d.

div.head: FRODSHAM POLICE NEWS.
div.p: FRODSHAM POLICE NEWS.

At Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, the follow- ing local cases wereheard : DRINK AND DISORDERLY.—Sampson Harvey, of very respectable appearance, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Church-st., Frodsham, on the 23rd inst.—Fined ss. and costs. _

IN'fritour TICKET. —Peter Kenyon was summoned for travaling on the Chester and Warrington Railway, on the 9th November, 1889, without having paid his fare. Mr. Preston prosecuted. He said the defendant was formerly an engine driver on the London and North-Western Rail- way. On the date named he entered a brake van at Helsbv, and told the guard, John Jones, that he had a ticket. Detective G. F. Whittick heard this answer given and followed him to Dunham Hill, where, when asked for his ticket, he said he had not one, and offered to pay his fare. This was refused.—Fined 10s. includ-

lug costs. CHARGE AGAINST A CLUB OFFICIAL AT HELSBY.— Charles Seymour. secretary of the Britannia Work Club, Helsby, was summoned for sellingbeer without a license, on the sth inst.—Mr. Churton represented the defendant. —P.C. William Brewster deposed to being on Chester main road, at Helsby, at 9.15 p.m., on Sunday, the sth inst. He saw a young woman named Elizabeth Julph come from the direction of the Britannia Club with a jug in her hand. He stopped her, and in consequence of what she said, he went to the club and saw the defend- ant behind the counter. He asked him if ha were the manager, and if he had served Julph with a pint of beer. Seymour replied "1 served a member of the club with it." Witness asked if he knew it was wrong to allow it to go off the premises to be consumed, and defendant said the club had sent the rules to the Excise Authorities, who had returned them without comment. A man I named Malcolm Butterfield said "I paid for it."—Mr. Churton characterised the case as a ridiculous and weak one. He Contended that Butterfield had a perfect right, as a member of the club, to purchase the beer, and give it to any person he desired, and it might be taken out if they so wished.—The Bench said the sale to the woman had not been proved to their satisfaction, and conse- quently the ease would be dismissed. The summonses against Malcolm Butterfield, and Elizabeth Julph, for aiding and abetting, were also dismissed.

div.head: ,IHEMICAL LABOURERS' UNION.
div.p: THE ,IHEMICAL LABOURERS' UNION.

WORKHOUSE (LOVES. I st V AN INerniNT. Birds love birds, and lads love lasses; The master foies his on sweet mistress; Teachers male love feinale teachers; And paupers love the Guardian features. Love is a gift from heaven above, The Bible teaches' God is Love.' God said man must not be alone; A help-meet made bone of his bone. To love, to comfort, and to bless, And make the illen of life grow less. A man without love in his soul Is doubly-blind as any mole. Mr. King explained that the title of the Union would " The Chemical Workers' and Labourers' Union of Great Britain and Ireland." and said as trustees they had two excellent gentlemen in Coun- cillor J. P. Mearns and Dr. Bellew. (Applause.) The rules provided that no strike should take place before the matter had heen discussed by the branch committees for the (listrict. He had been told that some Men Were afraid to associate with them be- cause they feared their masters but he could tell them that if a master committed any injustice to- wards anyone of their members, the Union could now retaliate, and would not be slow to do so. (Ap- plause.), The Union would soon be strong enough. to stopsatny man,from working who was not a mem- ber, and if anyone went to supply the places of those who Might be brought out on strike, they would be treated as blacklegs. The Union would not prac- tice, coercion, but they were anxious tn protect the Interestior their members as a body, and not as in- dividuals,--' He contended that much good had al- ready resulted from the formation of the Union, an 4 urged iteAims upon every individual chemical werker,Avho hadrnot yet joined its ranks. They had.novi, he said..over I,2ooinepzbers, and after the rules had been circulated they expected to have 1,500 in the course of the nettfortnight.
